The weather in Finland can change without warning; a balmy morning with blue skies might give way to sleet, snow, and harsh winds by lunchtime—which is why Finnish people tend to check the forecast often.  

And because temperatures can vary greatly between the southern and northern regions of the nation, local forecasts are essential. 

As one of the country’s largest media companies, Sanoma reaches millions each day with TV, radio, magazine, and newspaper content. It is adept at serving local audiences, yet its radio stations have until recently only offered national weather forecasts during its news broadcasts.

Sami Virtanen, Sanoma’s Content Insight Strategist for radio, says that while the company was keen to offer more locally focused forecasts, the business case for doing so was not strong enough. 

“It would have been quite expensive, having all these separate weather departments,” he says.   

But things changed radically last year when its two radio stations began airing local forecasts across 26 different regions, three times a day—all using AI technology from Microsoft. “We are now producing 78 additional forecasts a day, quickly and efficiently, for an audience of up to 200,000 people,” Virtanen says.

Each forecast is read by a lifelike synthetic voice created using the text-to-speech feature Custom Neural Voice (CNV), part of Azure AI Speech Service. Sanoma also uses Azure OpenAI’s GPT-4o to prepare the reports with data from the Finnish Meteorological Institute. 

“There was such a large volume of regional weather data that it would be a full-time job to manage it all manually,” says Renny Järvinen, Head of Sound Production at Nelonen Media, a subsidiary of Sanoma. “With AI we were able to fully automate the whole process.”

This transformation means that “Sanoma can offer a better product to listeners at a fraction of what it would have cost to do manually,” Järvinen says. It also creates opportunities to grow advertising revenues; local businesses can pay to be featured on one of the forecasts. And since the initiative is easy to expand, it is an enabler for efficient growth in the future. 

“It’s very scalable, so if we want to make our stations even more local, we have the capability,” Järvinen says. Sanoma also has plans to use CNV for certain news broadcasts.

Building AI initiatives on a foundation of trust 

Sanoma has a long history of keeping the Finnish public informed, with deep institutional expertise in providing accurate information—and multiple brands that have earned the trust of a wide audience. 

Amid concerns about the impact of AI on the media landscape, this is a major asset, says Pauli Tölli, Sanoma’s Chief AI Officer.

“Whatever we are doing with AI, it's good to remember that we started publishing newspapers in 1889,” he says. “We have lots of historical content, which is one reason why our first priority with AI is safe usage and intellectual property rights.”

As well as the weather forecasts, Sanoma has synthetic voices to read its news articles and AI-generated summaries of major events such as the last US election. It also uses AI to suggest headlines that get more clicks, and to save time in the news gathering process by summarizing information from its own published materials. 

Whatever the use case, Sanoma applies the same standards of rigor, transparency, and consistency to AI-generated content as it does to any of its output, he adds. For the weather broadcasts this means, among other things, an announcement informing audiences that they are AI generated. 

“We see that readers and consumers trust our news brands. We need to earn that trust every day,” Tölli says. 

Sanoma conducted a survey before launching the synthetic voice to determine listeners’ attitudes to the change. It found that only 11% of respondents had listened to news or audio articles read by an AI voice. On top of that, three quarters said they associated AI-generated media with artificiality and fakeness. 

Yet when respondents actually heard the synthetic audio samples played by Sanoma, the vast majority had a positive perception. “When they heard the voices, it sounded much better than they had probably expected,” Virtanen says. 

In a follow-up survey this year, Sanoma found audience perceptions of the synthetic broadcasts remained strong. Their Microsoft custom Supi voice outperformed other voices on the market in terms of perceived suitability: 70% said it suited news articles either fairly well or very well. On top of that, people were more likely to think it sounded like a human than a machine when asked to guess based on a sample.

Audiences are growing more familiar with AI in media

The earlier survey also gathered data about people’s perceptions of AI in the media generally. The majority, 57%, had a neutral attitude towards AI-generated media content, while 27% had a negative one. Respondents trusted AI-generated content from established media more than from less established sources online, but the results showed there was still a way to go in earning the trust of the majority.  

By using AI responsibly and transparently, Sanoma is working to build trust over time. “Since we took that survey last year, I think our audience has gotten more used to content generated with AI, and they can see that we have not generated any fake news or taken things in the wrong direction,” Virtanen says. “At the same time, it’s helping to make our products better and improve the audience’s experience.”

Issues are easy to resolve and output is consistent

To develop the AI weather service, Sanoma had to overcome several challenges. One issue was that every forecast had to be the same length so that they would fit into the live national news broadcast. 

“That was critical for our success because they needed to be on air at the same time and they needed to end at the same time,” Järvinen says. “But AI isn’t very good at estimating text length.” 

They solved this issue by designing each local weather report to consist of only five sentences, with each sentence defined by a strict prompt structure.

To train the voice itself, they used a base script from Microsoft and then added some of their own custom phrases—known as “training utterances”—to make it more relevant to weather reporting, amounting to a total of around 750 utterances. 

Another thing that the team found from its survey was that when the voice was based on a well-known broadcasting personality, listeners found it less convincing. “If we use the voice of someone famous, then listeners are always comparing it very closely to their own idea of the real thing,” Virtanen says. 

So instead, they trained the model using voices from previous presenters who were no longer well known.   

“Choosing the right human voice for the base recording was crucial,” Järvinen says. “This is where we have the advantage, because we work with voice and audio for a living. We have a lot of experience with this, and we have access to a wide range of voice talents in the Finnish market.”

During testing, the team noticed some pronunciation issues, which Järvinen says may have been due to the fact that Finnish is not widely spoken and there is consequently less testing with Finnish voices. 

“Microsoft helped us to address this issue promptly, and we received really great support from them.” 

Another benefit of opting for Microsoft, he adds, is that their CNV technology offers a higher level of reliability. 

“With other voices you can’t fully trust the output and you need constant human oversight, but with Microsoft’s neural voice, you don’t have to do that. If there is a problem, you can reproduce it and therefore you can fix it. That’s not the case for competitors, and it’s why this voice is best for us,” he says. “That means once it is fine-tuned, we can rely on it to perform consistently and accurately. So I think the neural voice is essential in a project like this, because the final result must always be high quality and predictable. We can't broadcast an unpredictable voice on radio or TV.”

This automated system allows Sanoma to produce localized forecasts across 26 regions.

Story Content:
Financial institutions seeking an advantage in today’s quickly evolving competitive environment face a common challenge: they are drowning in documents and bogged down by repetitive, manual tasks. From extracting data buried in PDFs to pulling figures from spreadsheets, these time-consuming and error-prone activities hamper innovation. To forge a smarter way forward for these organizations, LayerX is focused on prioritizing AI-driven automation technologies to support seamless interoperability and time savings.

The AI start-up began with a goal to build a B2B, AI-powered software as a service (SaaS) platform for enterprises that process an abundance of documents. The platform makes it possible to review any document, extract key knowledge, and translate it into a smart, searchable database that empowers users and AI to tap into any organization’s collective know-how.

As LayerX developed the concept, it prioritized finding a secure, cloud-based foundation to earn enterprise trust. It needed an AI-powered, scalable solution for document processing—one that could handle massive volumes with a high level of accuracy.

Choosing Azure to power Ai Workforce

LayerX saw the strategic advantage of Microsoft Azure. “We chose Azure from day one because of its smooth integration with Azure OpenAI models through Azure AI Foundry,” says Ryuya Nakamura, Executive Officer at LayerX. 

To bring the platform to life, LayerX built Ai Workforce, a tool that lets a document-heavy organization mine its documentation, quickly develop presentations, and automate repetitive tasks. Built on Azure, the platform takes advantage of its scalable, highly secure cloud infrastructure.

By adding Azure OpenAI in Foundry Models, Ai Workforce facilitates fast and seamless data exchange within the Azure ecosystem. The core generative AI processing in Ai Workforce is fueled by Azure OpenAI for knowledge sharing. It includes three other Azure AI Foundry products: Azure AI Document Intelligence for accurate optical character recognition capabilities, Azure AI Search for improved search, and Azure AI Translator for translating text and documents across multiple languages. “The advanced AI products in Azure AI Foundry, like Azure AI Document Intelligence, Azure AI Translator, and Azure AI Search, outperform those of other cloud platforms,” notes Nakamura.

To host Ai Workforce’s back-end applications in a fully virtualized environment, LayerX uses Azure Container Apps. “The dynamic session capabilities of Azure Container Apps allow us to spin up isolated environments on demand and run rule-based Python code more securely and at scale,” says Fumiya Shinozuka, Engineering Manager at LayerX. A key differentiator and advantage: each session runs in its own Hyper-V sandbox, providing enterprise-grade security and isolation. Each environment includes a Python code interpreter to dynamically execute rule-based logic in real time—ideal for processing specific customer requirements and other computer-intensive tasks.

LayerX also uses Container Apps for migration and reminder emails, creating two beneficial outcomes. For migrations, the company saves on costs because it’s needed only when migrating database schemas. For reminder emails, LayerX can use the service to effortlessly create scalable cron servers.

By using a consumption plan with Container Apps, LayerX achieves efficient, serverless horizontal scaling. The service seamlessly manages this scaling, while Azure Cosmos DB takes care of vertical scaling to meet data demands. Processes are executed as asynchronous jobs, allowing dynamic scalability. The company employs various AI solutions, including Azure OpenAI and Azure AI Document Intelligence, to process documents and store them in Azure Cosmos DB.

All users can review and edit the results. Users can also recover older data from the application. The Azure AI Translator API helps with multilanguage translation by detecting and instantly translating input language. Although LayerX’s enterprise customers are in Japan, the documents they work with might be sourced in other languages, such as Chinese or English.

Earning trust through uncompromising security 

Trust is everything for financial organizations. These institutions operate under some of the strictest data protection standards in the world, so any technology adopted must meet that threshold. That’s why security and compliance are foundational to Ai Workforce.

LayerX uses private endpoints in Azure so Ai Workforce customers can use an encrypted connection to keep traffic over a private IP within the customer’s virtual network. These network interfaces increase data protection and help ensure data stays localized.

Because several of LayerX’s clients are using other Azure products, ecosystem compatibility and seamless interoperability offer cost and time savings while maintaining strict compliance.

LayerX determined Azure Cosmos DB and its enterprise-grade security will help uphold the rigorous demands of the financial sector. “We plan to use the row-level security in Azure Cosmos DB to add an additional layer of protection, further ensuring that no tenant can access another’s data,” explains Shinozuka.

Faster processes and smarter presentations with AI personalization

Today Ai Workforce is transforming how financial institutions handle documents and processes, like preparing loan approvals and settling accounts. It also lets businesses fine-tune the AI to match their specific workflows, resulting in flexibility and management cost reduction. Timely document analysis accelerates loan approval times. The time it used to take manually reviewing documentation is much shorter, so settling accounts happens at lightning speed.

Organizations also save time working on presentation materials. Bankers and salespeople build pitch decks featuring company logos and financial data to present to clients. Due to strict privacy laws, they can’t access another person’s presentation, even within the same company. Companies still want to circulate presentations without customizing each in a bespoke manner, and Ai Workforce allows sharing at scale while maintaining compliance.

To securely store presentations in the presentation data lake, the creator must first anonymize the file. Ai Workforce identifies all images and texts and recommends company names, logos, financials, or charts to mask. Once the user anonymizes the presentation, it is sent for a security check. Once approved, the presentation is stored as an anonymized, downloadable presentation. To search for a presentation, the user specifies tags, and the platform uses Azure OpenAI and Azure AI Search to explore the database for a similar presentation.

The innovation journey continues

With Azure at the foundation of Ai Workforce, LayerX clients are already seeing measurable impact. For instance, credit risk solutions provider Mitsui & Co. Credit Consulting is experiencing significant productivity gains since adopting Ai Workforce.

Today, employees refine AI-generated drafts instead of manually editing and creating documents from scratch, freeing time for them to focus on advanced analysis and creative tasks. “We anticipate a reduction of 570 work hours annually,” says Hiroaki Takizawa, Manager of the Innovative Product Development Department at Mitsui & Co. Credit Consulting.

To stay at the forefront of AI technology, LayerX is using Azure OpenAI o4-mini reasoning models. “Newer reasoning models always help us realize more difficult but valuable use cases and deliver faster,” says Nakamura. LayerX has expansion plans into other document-heavy industries but is keeping busy in the financial sector. “Once one team in a company adopts Ai Workforce, others quickly follow for deep adoption,” says Ken Wakamatsu, Product Marketing Manager at LayerX.

Looking ahead, Nakamura envisions introducing Ai Workforce into the automotive manufacturing industry. “I’ve always admired the dynamic between Jarvis and Tony Stark (from Marvel’s Iron Man comics). Jarvis brought Stark’s ideas to life. We want to give every engineer in auto manufacturing their own Jarvis, empowering them to innovate like Stark. This is my vision,” concludes Nakamura.

Story Content:
“We are obsessed with the quality of what we do.”

Michele Carmina, Head of Group Digital Technologies at Generali and Head of Global Digital Factory at Generali Operations Service Platform, is describing the commitment to excellence that the company embodies.

Established in Trieste, Italy in 1832, Generali boasts an Italian heritage with an international outlook and now operates in over 50 countries serving over 70 million customers.

And when it comes to the latest efforts to strengthen their technology assets, having solutions that help their developers code better and faster, is key.

That's why the Italian behemoth - one of the largest global integrated insurance and asset management companies in the world - decided to adopt GitHub Copilot.

The prospect of using Generative AI tools like GitHub Copilot that were already integrated with the development environment used by its team was enticing, says Carmina.

With an existing relationship with Microsoft, the next step was a no-brainer for Generali.

“We want to improve efficiency and be faster in delivering our software projects, improve our overall business and achieve our strategic objectives by being more productive in all phases of the software development life cycle, with a special focus on coding," explains Carmina. And Microsoft was the perfect partner to help them get there.

Early success with experimenting

In early 2024, Generali successfully launched GitHub Copilot in Italy, Germany, and France. It’s now being used by about 2,000 of their developers.

The company began defining concrete targets in terms of efficiency that every country of the group could achieve by adopting the technology in the software development cycle and in particular their coding.

It really took off later in 2024.

One of the key factors of their success was the ease of integration into the development environment. In particular, developers found the Autocomplete and chat function of GitHub Copilot to be highly beneficial tools that they say have helped amplify and augment the capacity and effectiveness of their developers.

Since implementing, they’ve been able to increase both the capacity and velocity to write code with higher efficiency than before.
“The possibility for the developers to start using this tool and see the results without any change in the way they work was a game-changer,” says Carmina.

But what came as a surprise to Carmina was the reaction from developers, who demonstrated an attitude in line with the thinking of “Now I've seen the benefits, and I cannot survive working without it anymore,” in Carmina’s own words.

Collaboration was key

The process with Generali has been collaborative and continuous with an open flow of feedback. For example, Generali and Microsoft hosted a hackathon in Milan with developers from across the company that proved critical to Generali’s success adopting the technology.

“We are focused on all the phases of the software development lifecycle with the objective to augment the capacity of our people to be supported by the technology, to do better, to do part of the work automatically, and to have more time to review what has been done,” says Carmina.

Generali says this collaborative effort will be an integral part of maintaining success moving forward.

Adopting GitHub Copilot is just the first step in an innovative strategy they plan to continue to iterate and evolve with. The company’s vision in terms of technology is to equip all of its developers with the tools to help accelerate and improve their work.

“We want to be flexible and fast enough to test these technologies very quickly, to have a clear vision, and to adopt it rapidly when we believe that it can bring value,” says Carmina.

Story Content:
The Royal College of Surgeons of England (RCS England) is pioneering the use of technology in the not-for-profit sector to drive value. Having already embraced Microsoft Azure and Microsoft 365 to support flexible and agile work, the organisation is now exploring Microsoft 365 Copilot, as it seeks to harness the power of secure AI to elevate employee experience and enhance the delivery of its mission to support the surgical profession in England.

“We want to encourage our employees to be more curious and familiar with AI, but the biggest barrier is data protection,” says Kim Lewry, Digital Delivery Senior Programme Manager at RCS England. “Microsoft 365 Copilot is the clear choice for us as it contains enterprise data protection, alleviating our fears around data exposure and ensuring compliance with regulations such as GDPR.”

Measuring value to drive adoption

To establish which roles would most benefit from Microsoft 365 Copilot, RCS England launched its adoption with a limited trial in different business areas.

Kim Lewry reflects, “During the pilot stage, we did a lot of reading and attended webinars to understand which roles would really benefit from Copilot licences. We started small and used Microsoft Forms to gather feedback and ask people to share their success stories. This has been a great way to build a community, troubleshoot and share best practice.”

The pilot demonstrated increased time savings and a strong return on investment, with 71 percent of employees reporting an increase in productivity. Copilot's ability to transcribe and summarise meetings has been transformational. In an environment where daily collaboration is essential, this delivers real value for the organisation, enabling employees to save time, gain focus, take more accurate minutes and more precisely list actions.

“Copilot is enabling people to be more strategic with their time and thinking,” says an end user at RCS England. “In meetings, for example, it's fantastic to be able to listen and participate instead of worrying about taking notes. Copilot enables me to focus on being present and engage more fully with my colleagues.”

Based on this success, RCS England extended Copilot availability to more employees, especially those responsible for taking minutes or with diary or email overload, such as admin roles and directors.

Enhancing collaboration, focus and precision

“The key to our success has been taking an incremental approach,” says Kenny Webster, Head of Learning Operations at RCS England. “Providing Copilot licences to individuals in each business area allowed them to learn and highlight the benefits to the rest of the organisation, as we continue to expand adoption.”

The availability of Microsoft Copilot in the business and productivity applications RCS England teams use every day is another key success factor. It encourages daily use and makes it easy for staff to identify new ways of working. Some users rely on Copilot to create formulas in Microsoft Excel while others use Copilot create content in Microsoft PowerPoint.

“I used to spend hours categorising, putting data into themes and analysing tranches of data from collaborative meetings,” says Kim Lewry. “Now, I’m using Copilot in Microsoft Whiteboard to help me brainstorm and do retrospectives. Copilot is saving me so much time, offering suggestions and helping me to analyse much faster and with greater precision.”

Time savings per user average at over two hours per week, with some people reporting time savings from their use of Copilot of up to five hours per week. The willingness of RCS England to innovate is boosting productivity and leading to a better employee experience, with average user satisfaction scores with the technology of 7.4 out of 10.

Cutting the time of data analysis

RCS England is also using Microsoft 365 Copilot to optimize the delivery of its high-quality training to students and members. It has found Copilot useful when assessing the large amounts of data in learning operations.

“In the learning team, we work with lots of curricula,” says Kenny Webster. “Just being able to tell Copilot to take a complex, impenetrable curriculum document and compare it to another document or webpage is wonderful. It saves time and the quality of output is better, as nothing is missed.”

In addition, the learning operations team is using Copilot to identify trends in student feedback. RCS England can better understand its students, ensuring its services align with expectations.

Kenny Webster explains, “My team sends over 1,500 feedback forms to our students every single year. To understand trends in this data, we’ve been using Copilot. We’ve found Copilot is wonderful for analysing huge amounts of text to identify the themes coming out of it.”

Supporting accessibility and inclusivity

The RCS England team is now using Microsoft 365 Copilot to support a more accessible, inclusive workplace and ensure that customer-facing and internal content is accessible for all. This includes analysis of both design and content.

Kim Lewry explains, “As part of a website audit, our digital team is using Copilot to assess the language on each page to make it accessible for everyone. I’ve also noticed it gives me accessibility warnings in PowerPoint when I use certain colours or text on certain colours. I think that’s a great feature.”

Kenny Webster agrees, “I’m using Copilot to make the language I use in job descriptions more gender neutral. I ask it to remove masculine phrases which might put off women from applying to a role.”

Leading AI innovation in the not-for-profit sector

RCS England is pioneering the use of AI in the not-for-profit sector. Its rollout of Microsoft 365 Copilot is encouraging employees to be AI-curious without undermining data protection. The responsible and incremental approach to adoption ensures the organisation achieves a strong ROI.

Kim Lewry explains, “The great thing about Copilot is that enterprise data protection is included in the licence – we don’t need to invest in additional security. I think this will help other organisations in the not-for-profit sector too, as we all have limited resources. This is a real positive from Microsoft.”

RCS England continues to innovate. Next, it plans to use Copilot Studio to build agents that will automate customer service, admin and HR tasks, driving further efficiency for its workforce and members.

“Agents are the next step in our journey,” explains Kim Lewry. “We have plans to integrate agents into our website and CRM to improve customer service and deliver on our mission to support the surgical profession.”

To continue this highly successful journey, RCS England is investing further, increasing its Copilot licences so that more employees can explore this exciting new technology and continue to drive greater value for the organisation and its members.

Johor Corporation (JCorp), the principal development agency of the Johor State Government, plays a central role in advancing Johor’s economic and social agenda. With over USD5 billion in assets and a presence across wellness and healthcare, agribusiness, real estate and infrastructure, and food and restaurants, JCorp’s journey is guided by the philosophy of Membina dan Membela—creating value, enabling sustainable communities.

Building a cohesive digital core

When Johor Corporation embarked on the task of strengthening operational cohesion across its diverse business units as part of its digital transformation initiatives, its priority was clear: eliminate silos, simplify communication, and enable faster access to reliable data. “We began with a very simple principle—speed matters,” says Budiman Bujang, Deputy Chief Digital Officer at JCorp. “Improving how we connect systems and people helps reduce the time between insight and action.”

A key part of this process was centralizing JCorp’s digital architecture to establish a single source of truth across its entities. Microsoft Azure, already part of the Group’s ecosystem, offered a natural path to integration—enabling a secure, scalable foundation without incurring additional cost. Business intelligence dashboards, powered by Power BI, replaced traditional reporting slides, allowing senior leaders to focus on insight rather than data collation. “Meetings became more focused. Leadership discussions are now anchored on real-time data, which has significantly improved clarity and response time,” adds Budiman.

Balancing integration with strategic autonomy

A broader migration to Microsoft 365 helped remove communication bottlenecks across healthcare, agribusiness, property, and food and restaurants verticals. But the emphasis wasn’t on tools alone—it was about embedding a collaborative culture, one that respected the distinct operating environments of each division while aligning them on shared outcomes.

The shift to secure digital infrastructure—leveraging services such as Microsoft Sentinel and Defender—also reflected JCorp’s emphasis on governance and trust. “Security is not a checklist item—it’s a foundational discipline that guides our digital decisions,” Budiman notes.

AI as an enabler, not a destination

JCorp’s next step involved scaling its use of AI to support high-accuracy decision making, innovation, and operational efficiency. Microsoft Copilot was rolled out as part of a broader shift towards AI-enabled workflows—from content generation and documentation automation to data-backed scenario planning. “JCorp workforce is taking advantage of generative AI integrated with our own enterprise data to get more insights and context from our knowledge repository,” adds Budiman. 

To support adoption, the organization introduced internal workshops, learning sessions, and prompt competitions. Early use cases were tracked and refined for impact. Today, more than 500 employees across JCorp use Microsoft 365 Copilot in their day-to-day workflows. Over 100 use cases have been mapped, with deployment phased based on operational need and functional relevance.

One example is the enhancement of JCorp’s document management system, where all records are now managed through an AI-enabled Records Management System. By combining generative AI with agentic AI capabilities, the platform automates repetitive tasks, streamlines document classification, and improves the accuracy of storage and retrieval—removing the need for manual intervention. This shift enables staff to focus on higher-value work, improving productivity and creating more meaningful impact across the organization.

JCorp is also using generative AI to simulate organizational personas, helping the company test ideas, map capabilities, and align proposals against real constraints like budgets and targets. “This is part of our efforts to promote a structured innovation process from idea generations, use-case development, and minimal viable product (MVP) production,” adds Budiman. “AI supports our ability to explore scenarios more quickly, assess feasibility, and improve how teams generate ideas that align with our direction.”

JCorp’s Enterprise-level Agreement (EA) helped simplify digital operations across its subsidiaries—reducing licensing complexity and aligning capabilities under a single, secure digital architecture. These efficiencies have supported faster adoption, clearer governance, and better resource deployment across the Group.

Looking ahead

As JCorp continues to evolve, it is also integrating tools like Dynamics 365 to support its finance operations. But more than the platforms themselves, the focus remains on cultivating a digitally mature organization—one that prioritizes clarity, speed, and insight. “Technology is only one part of the equation. The real shift comes from how we apply it to serve our purpose, transforming our people to become digitally fluent,” Budiman reflects. This mindset—strategic, structured, and focused on long-term value—anchors Johor Corporation’s digital approach. It is defined not by dependency, but by discernment.

Seegene is a total PCR molecular diagnostics solution provider with a corporate vision of creating "a world free from all diseases.” In 2020, when the COVID-19 pandemic swept across the globe, Seegene successfully developed a diagnostic assay in just two weeks, significantly raising the profile of Korea’s pandemic response, often referred to as “K-quarantine.” Operating seven subsidiaries worldwide, Seegene generates 90% of its revenue from overseas, firmly establishing itself as a global company.

Seegene's proprietary syndromic qPCR test is the only technology in the world capable of detecting 14 pathogens that cause similar symptoms in a single tube, even providing quantitative values on disease severity. In 2024, Seegene launched a technology-sharing initiative in collaboration with Microsoft and Springer Nature to foster collaboration with life scientists around the world.

Advancing a technology-sharing initiative through partnership with Microsoft

YS Baeg, Senior VP of Corporate Strategic Planning at Seegene, emphasizes the importance of the company’s partnership with Microsoft in pushing forward its technology-sharing initiative. “Azure AI drives automation of Seegene’s core research, enabling global experts—even without PCR experience—to contribute based on their expertise. Azure HPC also accelerates genome analysis, supporting simultaneous global collaboration.”

Seegene chose Azure AI not only for its performance, but also for its strong compatibility with widely used global tools. Considering the integration with global standard tools like Microsoft 365, the company believed it could gain a competitive edge quickly. For effective data sharing with global partners, a highly compatible platform was essential, and Azure provided both universality and a strong global track record.

Seegene also adopted Azure HPC (High Performance Computing) for its genome analysis processes. HPC is a computing technology used primarily for handling large-scale parallel processing tasks, such as complex computations, analysis, and simulations. With Azure HPC, Seegene was able to address two major challenges. The first was scalability: expanding its on-premises HPC infrastructure not only faced physical limitations but also required significant capital investment. By transitioning to Azure, Seegene gained the flexibility to scale according to workload demands, offering a significant cost advantage. The second was compliance and disaster recovery. As Seegene expands globally, meeting country-specific regulations and implementing robust disaster recovery systems is crucial. In this regard, Microsoft provides trusted infrastructure and deep experience, instilling confidence in Seegene’s operations.

Transforming Research and Analysis with Azure AI and Azure HPC

Beyond these overall benefits, what matters most for Seegene is the transformation of its R&D processes. Seegene’s product development is structured into three stages: the first is basic research, followed by in silico simulation to pre-validate candidate gene sequences, and finally, the production and testing of actual products.

Kim DoHee, General Manager of IT Strategy Group at Seegene, says that adopting Azure AI has maximized the efficiency of data analysis work. “Previously, manual analysis required four experts working for a month to plan a diagnostic product. With Azure AI, a non-expert can now complete the task in a day—reducing workload by 75% and greatly improving efficiency. Large-scale gene analysis time is also expected to drop from 7 hours to 20 minutes.”

Through its Azure AI-based development platform, Seegene anticipates being able to collaborate with over 40,000 researchers globally and develop more than 1,000 diagnostic assays simultaneously. In the initial research phase, Azure OpenAI helps analyze vast amounts of academic papers and web content quickly. These documents are first converted into vector databases, with PDF files being digitized using Document Intelligence. Azure AI Search is then used to extract relevant data efficiently, and the GPT engine of Azure OpenAI summarizes the key points. In addition, custom AI agents are generated based on specific analysis objectives to improve precision.

While every stage of R&D is important, the pre-validation of gene sequence compatibility is considered the core process. Jay Ryu, Director of IT Strategy Group at Seegene, states that Azure HPC has helped them accomplish this task effectively. 

“In silico refers to a computer-based simulation process that identifies candidate target gene sequences and determines their optimal combinations. Using Azure’s AMD-based high-performance computing, we enable distributed processing—greatly accelerating analysis and boosting research productivity.”

A Roadmap Co-Designed by Seegene and Microsoft

YS Baeg emphasizes that collaboration with Microsoft has become an integral part in realizing Seegene’s corporate vision and expanding its business. 
“What’s most satisfying about working with Microsoft is not just Azure’s performance and security. Through the Innovation Hub and Unified Support programs, Microsoft has offered tailored guidance and expert support—proving to be a true business partner throughout our journey.”

Seegene plans to expand its business model across all domains by sharing its unique syndromic qPCR development technology, enabling scientists worldwide to contribute to its mission of “a world free from all diseases.” To support the massive data analysis this initiative will require, Seegene completed a 2024 proof of concept (PoC) validating Microsoft Fabric, an AI-based data platform. Built on the Azure ecosystem, Seegene will continue to collaborate closely with Microsoft through every stage of its innovation journey from development and regulatory approval to marketplace deployment, growing together.

SharePoint houses a multitude of organizational resources. It is the place where store associates find customer policies, technicians find instruction manuals, and nurses find the latest health protocols. We know that the answer is in SharePoint, but finding the exact piece of information you need can prove difficult and time-consuming.

For Amey, a leading provider of engineering, operations, and decarbonization solutions across the United Kingdom, finding accurate answers quickly is imperative to keeping their frontline safe. With SharePoint agents, their employees can use their mobile device to send a chat, in whatever language they speak, and receive a response about health and safety policies in seconds. If further information is required, they can ask follow-up questions or use the cited direct links to the original, organization-approved documentation retrieved by the SharePoint agent.

Andy Richards, Chief Digital Information Officer for Amey, said: “The introduction of SharePoint Agents marks a significant leap forward in making innovative technology accessible to everyone in our organization, particularly for our frontline workers. With 99% of our data stored across 180 million SharePoint files, accessing critical information like safety policies can be slow and inefficient, requiring employees to leave their work site to search manually.

Now, employees can instantly access vital information via a simple chat on their mobile devices, transforming the way we work. This innovation is improving efficiency, enhancing safety, and boosting confidence among our teams, empowering them to deliver better outcomes for the UK’s communities we serve every day.” SharePoint agents are currently accessible via SharePoint sites or Teams.

Learn more about how Amey is using SharePoint agents to support their front-line workers at YouTube.

Virgin Money has 6.6m retail and business customers across the UK and offers a range of straightforward, award-winning products. It has been part of the Nationwide Building Society since October 2024, creating the UK’s first mutual full-service banking provider. With a purpose of banking – but fairer, more rewarding, and for the good of society, Virgin Money is taking that ambition further, partnering with Microsoft to drive innovation at scale and deliver smarter, faster banking experiences.

Making every customer touchpoint count

Virgin Money believes great banking begins with great conversations. That’s why the organisation puts customers at the heart of everything it does, aiming to make every interaction fast, easy and seamless.

“We’re focused on resolving issues at the very first point of contact,” says Alison Lattimer, Head of Customer Service Operations at Virgin Money. “When a customer reaches out, our aim is to resolve their query first time, every time.”

To bring this vision to life, Virgin Money partnered with Microsoft, embracing the power of AI agents with Microsoft 365 Copilot and Microsoft Copilot Studio. Together, they developed Redi – an AI-powered agent designed to transform how Virgin Money serves its customers.

“We chose Copilot Studio primarily for the powerful capabilities it offers through the Power Automate platform,” explains Ruaridh Wallace, BizApps Centre of Excellence (COE) Lead at Virgin Money. “What started as basic chatbots in our virtual agents has evolved into a fully integrated AI solution.”

Transforming customer interactions

Redi is reshaping the way Virgin Money connects with its customers, making service more proactive and precise. Whether it’s answering questions or anticipating needs, the AI assistant plays a key role in improving the experience at scale.

Take something as simple as a replacement card notification. When a customer is due to receive a new card, Redi automatically sends an outbound message and confirms their address – a small interaction that delivers big results.

Laura MacLeod, Product Strategy Senior Manager at Virgin Money, reflects, “Engagement for these messages sits at around 54%. That means over half of our customers choose to interact, and of those, 97% complete the journey from start to finish.”

And that impact shows up in the feedback too. “A lot of customers are very satisfied with their experience using Redi,” adds Alison Lattimer. “We see that reflected clearly in our customer satisfaction scores.”

By reducing friction and increasing responsiveness, Redi is building trust, one conversation at a time.

Empowering people, scaling service

While Redi is transforming customer experiences on the front end, it’s also becoming an indispensable ally behind the scenes, supporting Virgin Money’s teams and enabling them to deliver better service, faster.

Alison Lattimer enthuses, “My team sees Redi as another colleague. It’s the one who passes a customer to them when a human touch is needed.”

By handling routine requests and triaging more complex ones, Redi frees up employees to focus on what matters most - delivering empathy, resolving high-impact queries and building relationships.

And the benefits don’t stop there. Redi also delivers actionable insights that help the organisation continuously refine its services.

Corinne McCulloch, Team Manager at Virgin Money, explains, “By using the insights that Redi provides, we’re able to build on the customer experience.” 

“It gives us the scalability and reliability we need – all within a native service layer,” adds Ruaridh Wallace.

Building the future of finance

With Microsoft’s support, Virgin Money is accelerating into the future, modernising its services, streamlining operations and setting a new standard for customer experience in financial services.

Laura MacLeod says, “We’ve been able to move away from old-style chatbots and toward more conversational banking. We’ve consolidated multiple virtual assistants into a single, smarter experience.”

The impact hasn’t gone unnoticed. Laura MacLeod continues, “We won an award for Best Use of AI in Financial Services, in the cards, payments and services category.” 

But for Virgin Money, the journey is just beginning. The team continues to build on its success with innovation, purpose and customer value at the core.

“Having integrated chatbots and back-end services allows us to deliver the kind of customer value and experience we truly pride ourselves on at Virgin Money,” concludes Ruaridh Wallace.

Learn more about Virgin Money’s inspiring AI transformation in this episode of the Microsoft Customer Series.

Story Content:
A new kind of programmer

At KUKA, a global automation leader and robotics manufacturer, the traditional approach to robot programming—requiring advanced technical training and fluency in proprietary code—no longer felt sustainable. The company had a bold new vision: what if automation didn’t require advanced training in proprietary robot programming languages? What if more people, from operators to planners, could contribute, adapt, and innovate without needing to start from scratch? This vision aligns with KUKA’s mission: to build intuitive automation solutions that simplify work across more applications. Whether through the company’s iiQWorks platform or an AI agent, the goal is the same: making automation easier and more accessible.

Building a solution for speed, safety, and access

KUKA worked with the Microsoft Industry Solution Engineering team to jointly develop the iiQWorks.Copilot, an AI-powered assistant that helps users generate code that programs robot movements with natural language prompts. Integrated into KUKA’s iiQWorks simulation platform, the agent allows users to design, test, and deploy programs in a digital environment, reducing setup time and improving safety before any hardware is installed. 

The solution is built using Microsoft Azure. With Azure OpenAI in Foundry Models, the company accesses GPT-4o to power the natural language interface. The assistant uses retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to fetch relevant KUKA data to generate accurate answers. Azure AI Search indexes internal content to support accurate responses. Azure SQL Database and FastAPI handles secure storage and data exchange between the front end and back end.

To meet internal compliance needs and protect intellectual property, KUKA runs the model in its own environment. “We host the model to help protect our data and IP,” says Christian Schwaiger, Technology Strategy Lead in the Corporate CTO Office at KUKA. “The Microsoft platform gave us the flexibility and enterprise-grade security we needed.”

A new tool for every user

With iiQWorks.Copilot, internal users at KUKA have seen programming time for simple tasks reduced by up to 80%, accelerating deployment and reducing reliance on specialized skills. By simplifying the programming process, the agent will significantly broaden who can contribute to automation.

For a technician, iiQWorks.Copilot will reduce the friction of trial and error. Instead of flipping through hundreds of pages of documentation or waiting on support from a programming team, they can adjust on the fly—like changing a robot’s grip pattern or timing—then simulate those changes safely before deployment. That keeps production moving and reduces downtime.

For planners and maintenance teams, the ability to experiment and adapt code will unlock faster collaboration and quicker troubleshooting.

Scaling impact with AI

iiQWorks.Copilot will support a wide range of users throughout the robotics life cycle. Factory planners can build and simulate robot workflows in the office, while technicians can adjust robot behavior during commissioning. Maintenance teams can update programs in response to new production demands. All changes are tested in simulation to safeguard performance and reliability. 

By expanding access to programming, the agent helps address a workforce challenge: the shortage of skilled labor. “This doesn’t replace programmers—it supports them and brings others into the fold,” says Schwaiger.

Just as important, the collaboration with Microsoft builds trust with customers. “Having Microsoft and KUKA collaborate is a sign of reliability. Customers want to know what’s behind the AI solution and that it’s safe,” says Emilio Galopin, Software Product Manager at KUKA.

Meeting the future of automation

As manufacturers push toward greater agility, flexible production lines, and smaller batch sizes, demand is growing for tools that make automation easier to adopt and adapt. KUKA’s agent is not just a time-saver but a step toward a more inclusive, responsive industrial future in which more people across roles can program robots.

“In the future, AI will play a major role in making access to, and use of, automation and robotics as easy as possible for more and more people in a wide variety of working environments,” says Reinhold Gross, CEO of KUKA Robotics. Looking ahead, KUKA sees iiQWorks.Copilot as a foundation for broader AI integration—one that helps bring automation to its customers more efficiently and more safely.

Bupa helps millions of people across the UK, Spain, Latin America, and the Asia-Pacific (APAC) region live healthier, longer lives. As a global leader in health insurance, health services, and aged care, the company is making quality care more accessible while advancing innovation to improve well-being at every stage of life. With AI reshaping healthcare, Bupa APAC saw an opportunity to make customer experiences more seamless, proactive, and personalized, from automating claims processing to developing preventative care plans tailored to individual needs. However, realizing this vision requires more than just technology; it demands a workforce equipped with the right skills. “We knew AI could be a powerful tool, but we needed to ensure our people were prepared to use it responsibly and effectively,” says Madeleine Jones, Digital and Data Learning Product Owner at Bupa APAC.

Bupa APAC embeds AI skilling into its strategy

“Our vision is to use AI to support our customers in the pursuit of our purpose, which is helping them live longer, healthier, and happier lives,” says Ed Falconer, Chief Data Officer at Bupa APAC. “It’s about how we use the data that we have on our customers to fulfill that promise. We want to support clinicians and patients to make better decisions, spend more time together, and create more personalized, preventative care plans.”

Bupa made skilling central to its strategy evolution. “AI is a critical part of our transformation, but technology alone isn't enough,” says Akhil Mittal, Cloud Platform and DevOps Manager at Bupa APAC. “Our focus has been on building the right skills and governance to make AI effective across the organization.”

To do that, Bupa created a Center of Enablement that aligned risk, legal, technology, and business teams to develop a unified approach to responsible AI use. “We brought together people from across the business to understand how to harness AI while ensuring responsible and ethical use,” says Jones. This early collaboration ensured alignment between AI ambition and the needs of different functions, laying the foundation for a tailored, role-based skilling strategy supporting the business priorities.

Programs designed for every role

With this foundation in place, Bupa APAC built out a skilling structure designed to meet people where they are. Senior leaders participated in programs such as Be a Data Leader, designed to help them understand the strategic role data and AI can play. Meanwhile, Bupa’s Edison platform—launched in 2021—serves as a central hub for digital and data capability-building, offering self-paced learning, instructor-led training, and a community of practice. “It was a very practical, hands-on approach,” says Jones. “We measured success not through hours completed, but through application of knowledge.” That model now extends into AI skilling.

Technical employees participated in more intensive training, including an AI semester focused on Azure OpenAI and GitHub Copilot. Developers have already generated more than 410,000 lines of AI-assisted code using GitHub Copilot, with more than 160,000 lines accepted into production—an adoption rate of 15%.

Across the wider workforce, everyday AI fluency has become a priority through initiatives like Prompt Like a Boss and Microsoft 365 Copilot training. “We don’t need our frontline contact center workers to become data scientists,” says Jones. “It’s really about understanding what each group of employees needs to do better in their day-to-day work.”

From learning to impact

This targeted approach is reinforced through experiential learning. Events such as the Bupa global B-Disruptive hackathon have become a proving ground for practical application. “Our global hackathon allows people across Bupa to come together around an idea or an ambition to utilize AI to solve a given problem,” says Falconer. “Actually, it’s the participation that’s really valuable—everyone’s learning the practical applications of AI.”

“Our AI skilling program which has included mini hackathons supported by Microsoft has created an environment for people to not only learn AI skills, but also to use them to solve problems,” says Jones. During one of these targeted hackathons, digital teams developed a chatbot to support frontline agents that cut response times from minutes to seconds, boosted satisfaction, and freed up staff to focus on more complex queries. Using the AI Alan chatbot, employees have initiated more than 30,000 AI-driven chat interactions, with a 20% acceptance rate.

To support AI growth and application, Bupa APAC launched the AI Factory, a foundational platform that allows teams to test, develop, and safely operationalize AI solutions. By establishing clear guardrails, the AI Factory gives teams across the business a reliable path from idea to implementation, helping them turn experimentation into real-world innovation. 

The AI Factory also underpins the learning programs that foster this experimentation culture. Gareth Lees-West, Innovation Culture Lead at Bupa APAC, says the structure of these programs helps build confidence across the organization. “The learning pathway was designed to ensure participants leave with AI and digital skills they can take back into their daily roles,” he says. The results speak for themselves: more than 100 AI use cases have been identified, contributing to both operational efficiency and improved customer experience.

What’s next for AI at Bupa APAC

Looking ahead, Bupa APAC will continue expanding access to learning through new initiatives like Bupa Campus, a digital-first, high-quality skilling environment designed for its globally distributed workforce. “We’re really focused on tackling strategic capability gaps and making sure people are prepared for what’s next,” says Jones.

For Jones, the investment in learning is what turns Bupa’s AI strategy from ambition into action. “Digital and data capabilities, especially AI, will help us meet our strategic goals,” she says. “But having our workforce ready with the right capability is what makes that possible.” And as AI becomes more embedded in how Bupa delivers care, it’s the people behind the technology who will shape what healthcare looks like tomorrow.

“Our mission at CommBank is to build a brighter future for all,” says Dan Jermyn, Chief Decision Scientist at Commonwealth Bank of Australia. Commonwealth Bank of Australia (CommBank), one of Australia’s largest banks with approximately 17 million customers, is working to strengthen customer trust and security and tailor financial experiences in a rapidly evolving financial landscape. As customer expectations rise, the bank seeks to harness AI to develop smarter, more secure, and highly customized banking experiences at scale.

Recognizing that AI’s full potential depends on workforce readiness, CommBank launched a structured skilling initiative to equip employees with the knowledge and tools to apply AI effectively across the organization.

Building AI fluency across the workforce

To educate employees on how AI can drive real impact, CommBank launched a structured skilling approach through its democratizing “AI for All” initiative. By investing in hands-on learning and experimentation, the bank is equipping employees with the confidence and expertise to use AI in their daily work.

CommBank embedded AI skilling across all levels of the organization through three structured learning paths: Leading with AI, Working with AI, and Building AI. This approach empowers employees with the knowledge and tools to use AI effectively.

Leading with AI equips executives and senior leaders with the skills to guide AI adoption strategically, facilitating responsible implementation and alignment with business priorities.

Working with AI provides employees across departments with practical training to use AI-driven tools like Microsoft 365 Copilot to improve productivity and assist decision-making.

Building AI develops technical expertise among engineers, data scientists, and developers, offering specialized learning with tools like GitHub Copilot and Microsoft Power BI to create AI-powered solutions.

Collaborating with Microsoft for success

CommBank collaborated with Microsoft to equip its workforce with the skills needed for AI adoption through a range of Microsoft learning programs. With offerings like Microsoft Learn, the Microsoft Enterprise Skills Initiative (ESI), and a Microsoft AI Academy, participating employees gain practical experience that goes beyond theory. Through training sessions, interactive learning, and boot camps, they apply AI to real-world tasks, deepening their expertise. Employees are becoming AI champions, fostering a culture of continuous learning, sharing best practices, and supporting colleagues through office hours and peer-led knowledge-sharing. “Skilling is really important for us because people are at the heart of our organization,” says Jane Adams, Domain Lead HR Business Partnering Learning and Skilling at Commonwealth Bank of Australia. “We need to enable our people to engage with AI, use new tools, and embrace new ways of working.”

CommBank introduced Copilot so employees could explore ways to automate routine activities, improve operational flow, and free up time for problem-solving. For technical teams, GitHub Copilot can accelerate coding by generating AI-powered code suggestions, reducing development time, and improving accuracy.

Jermyn notes that Copilot is driving a shift in workplace dynamics. By reducing cognitive load from routine activities, employees are able to dedicate more time to strategic and innovative work. He notes, “With Microsoft 365 Copilot, early adopters reported saving 16% of their time by reducing repetitive tasks, allowing them to focus on more meaningful work and bring their best selves to what they do.” With 10,000 active Copilot users, the impact on CommBank’s business is tangible.

Strengthening AI capabilities for competitive advantage

Approximately 30% of GitHub Copilot AI-driven code suggestions are adopted by CommBank’s engineers, accelerating innovation and streamlining complex development processes. CommBank has also provided employees with opportunities to strengthen their analytical capabilities with AI-driven tools like Power BI. Through AI skilling initiatives, participating employees learn to use self-service analytics to interpret complex data and make informed customer decisions. By developing these skills, teams across the organization can confidently apply AI insights, to improve both efficiency and decision-making.

CommBank is exploring ways to use data, AI, and analytics technologies to reimagine experiences for its customers, communities, and colleagues. One example is Benefits Finder, an AI-powered tool that identifies government rebates and benefits customers may qualify for based on their responses to a few simple questions. It has helped connect customers to an estimated $1.2 billion in government rebates since 2019.

CommBank views its ongoing investment in AI skills as crucial to staying competitive in the rapidly evolving banking industry. “AI is transforming how we work, and the possibilities keep growing,” Adams concludes. “By continuously investing in AI skills, we’re empowering our people to stay ahead, innovate, and shape the future of banking.”

Worten, a major consumer electronics retail chain of the Sonae Group, faced significant challenges in accessing and managing internal operational documents stored in SharePoint. This hindered quick searches for critical information in stores, leading to inefficiencies in customer service. With over 240 physical stores across Portugal, the largest national e-commerce site, and 4,000 employees, Worten needed a solution to streamline their operations and improve customer satisfaction.

The Technological Challenge

Worten's employees had to search through an operations manual with over 1,000 loaded documents to find the information they needed to meet customer needs. The average search time for specific information was around 3.5 minutes, which added to the average customer service time. Considering the high volume of over 75,000 searches conducted annually, this inefficiency corresponded to around 11,000 hours of search time annually. Worten identified an opportunity for improvement and challenged their specialized Artificial Intelligence (AI) tech team to develop a technological solution in collaboration with Microsoft.

Microsoft Generative AI in Azure at the Core of the Solution

The solution involved implementing an advanced chatbot developed in partnership with EY, using the Azure AI platform. These technologies support the development of the solution by simplifying and accelerating the process while allowing adaptation to the specific needs of customers. The chatbot uses Azure AI Search for the search engine and Azure OpenAI for the conversational component. “Besides Microsoft being our partner, the AI Search and OpenAI services have very high quality within the market offerings,” says David Barros, Data Scientist at Worten. Microsoft and EY provided technical support and assistance to ensure the solution met Worten's requirements.

Satisfied Employees, Even More Satisfied Customers

The support chatbot for Worten employees, accessible via a smartphone, can answer any question related to store processes based on the information in the store process manuals. Along with the answer, a specific link to the manual is provided, allowing the employee to obtain a higher level of detail. The reduction in time invested in searching for essential information for efficient customer service is confirmed by the employees themselves. Now that the solution is in Production, the feedback has been very positive, with employees reporting that searching for documentation has become a much simpler process, from minutes to seconds. “Employees report that after the solution was implemented, searching for documentation became a much simpler process, from minutes to seconds. They save a lot of time,” says Eduardo Lucena, Product Owner at Worten.

From a Pilot Project to a Solution Across All Stores

The pilot project was tested in two Worten stores, specifically in the remote sales area. Worten is focused on developing the scalability of the project on two main fronts: ensuring the capacity of their servers to support the volume of operations of more than 200 Worten stores and generalizing the solution to apply to any type of documentation inherent to daily operations. The challenge was overcome by Worten, in partnership with Microsoft technology, saving more than 11,000 hours in the search process, which was converted into value on the sales floor, resulting in a higher number of sales at a lower cost.

Conclusion

Worten's implementation of Microsoft's OpenAI and Azure AI Search technologies revolutionized information search in stores, significantly increasing productivity and enhancing customer service efficiency. The collaboration between Worten, Microsoft and EY demonstrates the potential of AI and cloud technologies to transform business operations and deliver measurable benefits.

Genpact, a global advanced technology services and solutions company, partners with leading organizations worldwide, including many from the Fortune Global 500, to transform their biggest challenges into opportunities for resilience and growth.

With over 125,000 employees and operations spanning 30-plus countries, Genpact leverages its expertise in advanced technology to design, build, and transform businesses, creating lasting competitive advantages for its clients.

The need for a unified data platform

Over time, Genpact's business units developed a range of dashboards connected to different data sources. While these applications served their initial purposes effectively, as the business evolved, the need for integrated solutions became greater. Although Genpact had a central data warehouse, it lacked up-to-date AI capabilities. This presented an opportunity to enhance integrations between disparate applications, to enable a unified view of enterprise data and unlock the full potential of real-time insights and advanced analytics.

Genpact recognized an opportunity to enhance its data infrastructure to fully leverage emerging technologies like AI and Generative AI. By modernizing its data warehouse, Genpact aimed to drive innovation, accelerate digital transformation, and strengthen market competitiveness, ensuring a future-ready foundation for advanced AI capabilities.

Transitioning to Microsoft Fabric

Genpact began evaluating data solutions to support its evolving business needs. After a thorough review, Microsoft Fabric, the unified AI-powered data platform emerged as the ideal choice. Its comprehensive features for data storage, seamless integration with emerging technologies, and compatibility with Genpact’s existing Microsoft landscape made it the right fit.

Active support from Microsoft throughout the implementation process further cemented the decision. As Rajendra Rao, Head of Enterprise Data Office at Genpact, explains, "To truly scale and accelerate our internal transformation, we needed a unified, future-ready data platform. Microsoft Fabric provided the single source of truth we required to drive innovation and operational excellence. Starting with human resources, we have scaled its implementation across the organization."

The phased rollout began with HR processes, gradually expanding to functions like finance and sales. Today, Microsoft Fabric is fully operational at Genpact, delivering measurable improvements in data accessibility and analytics.

Harnessing agility and insights with Microsoft Fabric

Genpact has achieved significant benefits from the implementation of the Microsoft Fabric solution.

Unified data and AI integration

By adopting Azure Fabric OneLake as its enterprise storage, Genpact now supports Azure OpenAI use cases. With streamlined data architecture, the company has built products for HR and finance that rely on natural language queries, simplifying decision-making and reducing dependency on multiple reports.

Enhanced HR operations

The migration of HR applications such as compensation and benefits, human resources shared services, talent and competency review, rewards recognition, and learning and development to the Fabric data warehouse has centralized critical metrics related to attrition, headcount, and reskilling. These insights are now accessible via unified dashboards, enabling accurate reporting and cost optimization.

“Microsoft Fabric has been a game-changer. No more digging through various reports or spreadsheets—everything is now at our fingertips. It has made decision-making faster, easier and more data driven with real-time insights. It is also the perfect platform to roll out AI-powered insight bots, supporting our vision of becoming an AI-first company,” says Indira Sovakar, VP, Human Resources, Genpact.

Accelerated innovation Fabric’s AI-powered capabilities allow Genpact to leverage machine learning and big data to unlock innovation and accelerate digital transformation across departments.

Rapid deployment

Genpact successfully deployed the initial use cases in the finance function within six months, followed by the quick deployment of HR use cases within three months.

Data governance and compliance

Built-in governance tools enable compliance with industry regulations, safeguarding data integrity and security throughout the platform.

Driving operational excellence across functions

This unified data approach isn’t just transforming HR. It is equipping Genpact’s finance teams to streamline processes and achieve unparalleled data accuracy. By leveraging natural language queries powered by Fabric, the organization is unlocking greater efficiency and transparency, paving the way for more informed decision-making across departments.

As Manish Goenka, Vice President, Finance, Genpact, notes, “The Chat with Data solution, built on top of Microsoft Fabric, empowers business teams with rapid, multi-dimensional data insights, offering a seamless, one-stop platform to leverage insights for enhanced decision making. Its features enable swift access to critical information, enabling smarter and faster decisions.” To date, Genpact has migrated approximately 15 terabytes of data, connecting 300 Power BI reports to Microsoft Fabric and engaging over 1,000 active users.

The road ahead

Genpact plans to archive data from various applications into Microsoft Data Lake, creating a scalable and centralized storage system for future needs. Through its “client zero” initiative, Genpact is now refining its use of Microsoft Fabric internally before extending the solution to its clients, creating a robust and validated offering.

As Vidya Rao, CIO, Genpact, shares, “Microsoft Fabric has been a game changer for Genpact Enterprise functions by accelerating creation of a single source of good quality Enterprise data and enabling natural language-driven access and generation of AI and ML based actionable insights.”

By embracing Microsoft Fabric, Genpact has created a unified platform, unlocking new levels of scalability, efficiency, and innovation.

Story Content:
Art Basel has long been a global force in the art world, curating fairs that span continents and cultures. With fairs in Hong Kong, Basel, Paris, Qatar, and Miami Beach, the organization brings together nearly half a million artists, collectors, and fans each year. But as the scale and complexity of these events grew, so did the need for a more connected experience—one that could bridge the physical and digital worlds without compromising the integrity of the artworks. 

“Digital doesn’t replace the physical experience,” says Alain Brusch, Global Head of Digital Platforms at Art Basel. “We aim to amplify and enhance it.”

Art Basel knew it needed to evolve the experience to retain, attract, and grow its audience. It also needed to find a meaningful way to promote artists and art galleries, ensuring they would continue to find value in participating in its art fairs.

To do that, Art Basel envisioned a new kind of digital companion—one that helps visitors navigate the fair, discover new artists, and engage more deeply with art. The solution needs to be intuitive, secure, and fast. And it needs to put AI directly in the hands of art enthusiasts, artists, and galleries in a way that is both natural and valuable.

Understanding the complexity

Art Basel decided to build an app that would securely synthesize gallery, artwork, attractions, and dining and lodging details across five cities and thousands of galleries. The app would also allow visitors to get more information about the exhibited artworks via a camera scanning feature, the Art Basel Lens. The Art Basel team imagines a fair attendee using the camera in the app to photograph a sculpture, for example, then immediately receiving artist, gallery, and related information about the sculpture. What’s more, the team wants to make strides in offering proper attribution to artists and galleries, and make it easy to share the artwork information on social media or contact the gallery. 

The multiple complexities of the project require a sophisticated tech stack. It needs the scalability to adapt to different visitor loads throughout the year, the flexibility to ingest and produce different content formats, and the security to help ensure personal recommendations stay personal. Compliance considerations are also paramount, as Art Basel operates in countries where Global Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) policies are in place. 

A new canvas for connection

To bring the vision to life, Art Basel collaborated with UIC Digital and Valorem Reply to build AI-based engagement features in the app powered by Microsoft Copilot. The app includes a conversational AI companion for nuanced queries and personalized recommendations, along with the Art Basel Lens, a real-time artwork recognition feature. Under the hood, the app is a complex orchestration of Azure AI Foundry products such as Azure OpenAI in Foundry Models, Azure AI Search, and Azure Machine Learning, designed to deliver performance, scalability, and compliance across a global footprint.

“With Microsoft, we feel understood in our mission. We see eye to eye on what we can accomplish, and Microsoft has the capabilities to turn ideas into experiences,” says Brusch.

Synthesizing data across four cities and hundreds of galleries

From the beginning, one of the core challenges was data integration. Synthesizing information from hundreds of galleries and thousands of pieces of artwork means there’s no format standard. Information is available in Word docs, PowerPoints, photos, PDFs, and other formats.

“The data wasn’t built for this use case,” says Gabor Kajtar, Technical Director at UIC Digital, which helped build the app. “We had to centralize data from Microsoft Dynamics CRM, a custom CMS, and a homegrown artwork database, then make it accessible to the AI companion in a performant and scalable way.”

Azure Cosmos DB stores and safeguards structured and unstructured data, while Azure AI Search enables fast, semantic filtering and retrieval. Azure API Management serves as the gateway for all app interactions, and Azure Container Apps and Azure Functions power the serverless back end.

For quick, accurate language processing and content generation in the form of tailored recommendations, the app uses Azure OpenAI.

Microsoft was a deliberate, considered choice. “Azure gave us the tools to build, test, and deploy quickly. Everything was automated. That let us focus on solving real problems, not managing infrastructure,” says Kajtar.

Real-time artwork recognition with the Art Basel Lens

The Art Basel Lens, developed by Valorem Reply, UIC Digital, and Art Basel, allows users to scan artwork with their phone camera and instantly receive attribution details, including artist and gallery information. The content is formatted for multiple use cases, such as easy sharing on social media or getting in touch with the gallery directly to inquire about purchasing. Achieving this requires a sophisticated AI pipeline capable of processing images in under two seconds. 

“When someone takes a photo, we crop the image to isolate the artwork, generate embeddings, and search for a match in our vector index,” explains Sean Smith, Practice Lead, Data and AI at Valorem Reply. “If the similarity score is above an acceptable threshold, we return the match with metadata. All of that happens in about two seconds.”

The Lens uses AI vision for image analysis because of its advanced algorithms, which can separate features in an image. Machine Learning accelerates the training for the cropping models, and AI Search, chosen for its comprehensive set of advanced search technologies, performs the similarity search. Azure Functions orchestrates the workflow, and Azure Blob Storage and Azure Cosmos DB manage image and metadata storage.

“We trained the model on public artwork datasets and gallery-provided images,” says Smith. “We had to account for real-world conditions—poor lighting, odd angles, people standing in front of the art, and artwork of various shapes and sizes. The scalability and flexibility of Azure provided exactly what we needed.”

Security, compliance, and global scale

Given the international scope of Art Basel’s fairs, the solution must meet stringent requirements for data privacy, identity management, and regulatory compliance. All services run within the Art Basel tenant, with data encrypted at rest and in transit.

The global network of datacenters within Azure helps ensure low-latency performance across continents, while built-in compliance with GDPR and other standards gives Art Basel confidence in its data governance.

Brusch notes, “Microsoft’s enterprise-grade security and compliance posture was a key reason we standardized on the Azure platform. We need a partner we can trust to scale with us and protect our users.”

A foundation for the future

With the Art Basel Companion and Lens now live, the organization is already seeing signs of impact. Artists and galleries benefit from increased visibility and proper attribution. Visitors navigate the fair more easily and engage more deeply with the artworks. And the broader art community is exploring AI as a tool for discovery and connection.

“As a collector, cataloguing my collection, understanding trends, identifying similarities and connections across artists and galleries is important,” says Leo Tan, a private art collector in Hong Kong. “The Art Basel app helps me do all that with ease.”

“We’re seeing more engagement, more returning visits, and more time spent in the app,” says Brusch. “But more importantly, we’re seeing people use it in ways that feel natural—like asking the AI companion for recommendations or scanning an artwork to learn more.”

The app is also helping Art Basel prepare for the future. With a highly secure, scalable, and compliant foundation built on the Microsoft stack, the team is exploring new features like wayfinding, restaurant bookings, and year-round discovery experiences.

“We’re just at the beginning of our journey,” says Brusch. “The app is still in its infancy—it needs to grow. But we’ve built something that can evolve with our users and with the art world.”
