The Germany-based international aid nonprofit Malteser provides care for hundreds of thousands of people every day. In Germany, caring workers provide healthcare, visiting services for lonely people, access to warming centers, and more. In a rural area of Haiti plagued by landslides, they teach farmers sustainable agriculture practices to improve their community’s nutrition and reforestation techniques to restore the ecosystem. In mobile outreach clinics in Uganda, they provide testing, advice, and paths toward early intervention for sickle cell disease, improving the quality and length of life for many people with this condition. 

Each of these projects reflects Malteser’s mission of providing healthcare, humanitarian relief, and social services. The Germany-based nonprofit, which is an institution of the international Order of Malta, promotes health and dignity for all. “Everything we do at Malteser is about helping other people and doing good in the world,” says Merle Elsner, Organizational Development Manager at Malteser.

Like many mission-driven organizations, Malteser is facing a growing need for their services. Demographic changes, immigration patterns, and the frequency of crises worldwide increase demand for Malteser's help with health, disaster relief, gender equality, and more. Meanwhile, funding uncertainties and staffing difficulties put pressure on the nonprofit’s operations. Malteser is rising to the occasion by gaining efficiencies, finding creative solutions, and fueling innovation through Microsoft 365 Copilot.

“We give to the world in every way we can,” explains Thomas Berding, Chief Information Officer at Malteser. “We are finding new ways to offer our services and help communities with the support of technology.”

Serving communities through greater efficiency

“The combination of passion and compassion drives us at Malteser,” Elsner says. From elder care in Germany to establishing water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) infrastructure in Africa and Asia, the nonprofit always aims to do more for the communities they serve. They are maximizing their work by becoming even more productive with Copilot.  

About 500 office-based staff now use Microsoft 365 Copilot, saving a significant amount of their time through the AI assistant’s efficiencies. They delegate repetitive tasks, such as designing protocols, drafting project plans, writing emails, outlining job descriptions, and analyzing the risks and strengths of new proposals. They also use the tool to streamline administrative work, such as directing Copilot to summarize email inboxes and identify urgent messages. Human oversight over outputs ensures materials are in line with both Malteser’s priorities and culture. 

Staff use the saved time to focus on the work that drives Malteser’s mission. For example, one manager uses Microsoft 365 Copilot to create shift schedules for 50 workers who run a shelter for migrants. It used to take him hours to balance scheduling conflicts, but now he completes this recurring task in a few minutes. He has more energy and time for leading his team, coaching individuals, and developing an even better experience for the people they serve. As another manager says, “Copilot gives me more time for what I care most about: supporting persons.”

Malteser’s IT service team is using Microsoft 365 Copilot to respond to calls and tickets. They use a Microsoft agent, which draws from information in a SharePoint-based knowledge base, to troubleshoot issues and answer questions for thousands of staff. While the team is continuing to refine the solution, “we see they are able to support colleagues faster,” empowering the entire workforce to get back to their mission-moving work, Berding says.   

The productivity gains have made a clear business case for Microsoft 365 Copilot. “We have to be very careful with overhead spending because we invest the most possible on our services,” Elsner explains. “Copilot is a good investment because it improves the efficiency of our work.”

Collaborating on a shared vision

Malteser provides frontline services in more than 30 countries, enabled by behind-the-scenes support staff based primarily in Germany. With such a dispersed workforce, “technology in the Microsoft world makes us more connected,” Berding says. 

Teams use the Microsoft 365 suite to collect shared information and seamlessly collaborate on documents, presentations, and creative content. Knowledge banks document organizational norms, role responsibilities, project statuses, past projects, and future strategies to ensure continuity. That way, teams can continue to push important work forward even when staff go on vacation or switch roles. “When people have the information they need, they can make better decisions. That makes our work better,” Elsner says.

With the foundation of Microsoft 365, Malteser rolled out Microsoft 365 Copilot, which easily integrates into the platforms staff use every day. The AI assistant acts as an “external perspective” to help colleagues hash out differences, identify where competing ideas overlap, and find common ground, Berding says. "As an impartial party, Copilot can overcome personal tensions and help people look at conflicts differently,” he adds. 

Malteser leadership has noticed that younger generations prioritize collaboration in their work style, embracing the team approach that technology enables. Access to cutting-edge tools helps with recruitment, too. Malteser hiring managers have noticed that young workers in particular are attracted to the opportunity to work in an organization that leverages technology. They see investment in Microsoft 365 Copilot as an investment in the workforce.

“Technology is an important step to connect our resources and enable us to work together,” Elsner says. “That makes us much stronger.”

Innovating better ways to serve

Within the context of meeting rising demand for services, Malteser is always looking to optimize its work. The nonprofit is applying technology to create new approaches and encourage innovation as an organizational value. “Using AI tools aligns with our ambition to be a forward-thinking, modern organization,” Elsner says.

Microsoft 365 Copilot “democratizes knowledge” to empower everyone—not only IT experts—to leverage technology. For example, Elsner wanted to automate and streamline a routine process in her work driving organizational development. Copilot provided a step-by-step guide to creating a workflow within Microsoft Power Apps. “I don’t know everything Microsoft technology can do, but I don’t have to because I can just ask Copilot,” she says. 

Malteser staff also use Copilot as a brainstorming partner. They type or dictate their free-form ideas into a document, letting their imagination flow. Then they instruct Copilot to organize the material into a structured set of concepts and even action steps.  

Malteser staff feel comfortable using technology because they know sensitive client and organizational data is safe. “For our clients and our teams, it’s all about trust. With Microsoft, we know our internal data stays internal,” Berding says. Any information fed into Copilot stays in a closed system, unlike other generative AI models. “Our trust in Microsoft security grows every year.”  

That confidence frees Malteser teams to do their best work. “Our mission is always to spend more time helping people,” Berding says. “Copilot makes that easier.”

Story Content:
BT Group is keen to explore and exploit new AI technologies responsibly for the benefit of its customers and colleagues. Seeing Microsoft Copilot as a new opportunity to get more from the business’ existing investment in its Microsoft environments, BT Group initiated a trial of Microsoft 365 Copilot across different user groups in the organisation. 

“Within our trial, we allocated 45 Copilot licences to our Able2 network, which focuses on accessibility at BT Group,” explains Liam Canavan, Software Engineering Principal at BT Group. “It very quickly became clear how much difference Copilot makes to colleagues with different accessibility needs.” 

Transformational impact

“For most of my adult life, I’ve been the most dyslexic person in the room,” states Ian Chown, Senior Manager for Data Projects and Risks at BT Group. “I joined the trial of Microsoft 365 Copilot because of advantages that it offers for people who are neurodiverse.”

“Given the nature of the role I’m in, I was very hesitant about using other generative AI tools in the open cloud, given the data leakage and data security risks. I was excited to test Copilot to see whether we could gain the advantages of generative AI within all of the safeguards and guardrails we have in place in our Microsoft 365 environment.”

Respond more rapidly to colleagues 

Ian Chown began using Microsoft 365 Copilot in September 2023 and says it has exceeded his expectations. “Using Copilot has changed the way I work. I’ve always felt quite inadequate and anxious when sending emails to senior people and peers. Using Copilot, I can suddenly get messages across in a far more prompt and efficient way.”

Before using Copilot, Ian Chown would review the emails he sent to colleagues as many as three times each, usually with twenty-minute breaks between each review. For important communications, he would often ask a colleague to check the quality of his writing. Inevitably, this meant a delay on getting back to people, even on urgent projects.

“I very quickly saw the advantages of using Copilot,” reports Ian Chown. “Within the first quarter I was saving two hours per day by using Copilot to draft and review all my correspondence. I’ve not had the same two hours offline at the end of every day where I was reviewing documents and going through the embarrassing circle of getting peer reviews. I’ve been a lot more confident when emailing people. I can respond to emails much faster – within two minutes instead of taking two hours.” 

Supporting colleagues with neurodiverse needs

Like Ian, users across the business have reported productivity improvements. The productivity boost averages around 72 minutes per week per person in the first quarter, rising to two hours per week per person once the user’s Copilot use is more embedded. Liam Canavan estimates that it takes around six to nine months to become fully comfortable with using Copilot, so that you can creatively adapt it to assist in any task.

He says, “For our Able2 user group, Copilot is so much more. It’s removing stress from the job. It’s helping them to feel they are performing better. There’s a real wellbeing aspect to using Copilot and we’re getting that message loud and clear.”

Stress-free creation of professional documentation

For Ian Chown, writing formal documents could be even more stressful than drafting emails.

“When writing a report or document, most of my peers would go through one round of review,” he explains. “In contrast, my reporting writing would require more scrutiny. A document could go through as many as four review stages.”

Today, Ian’s use of Copilot has transformed this process.

He explains, “My report-writing process is now two-and-a-half days quicker than if I did it without Copilot. I use a combination of dictation and then Copilot to edit, using the prompting to go back through and refine paragraph by paragraph. When I submitted one recent document for peer review, it passed first time. I’ve never felt more comfortable in my role because, with the support of Copilot, I can literally do things straightaway.”

Everyone can reach their full potential

“Copilot is now integrated into everything I do,” continues Ian Chown. “I’ve always been ambitious, but I would probably now apply for a broader spectrum of roles, including those outside my comfort zone.”

While Ian’s horizons are expanding, the good news for the business is that he feels happier at BT Group than ever. 

“I’ve never felt as comfortable psychologically as I have in the last six months,” Ian Chown enthuses. “For me, Microsoft 365 Copilot is an anchor to BT Group at the moment. I wouldn’t want to go to another company that doesn’t use Copilot. I fear the day that we lose our licences.”

A wider roll-out at BT Group

While the Able2 group trial has been most immediately successfully received, BT Group is currently exploring use cases for other user groups. Work is ongoing to understand the potential for different departments and personas, assessing how Copilot could augment each role and aiming to put a number on the productivity savings that could be achieved by rolling out Copilot.

The BT Group team is extremely creative in how it communicates with these users. As well as producing short, engaging videos on different Copilot topics, it sends out a daily email containing a prompt to try out each day. These are usually fun ideas to spark people’s imagination, such as asking Copilot to identify your superpower based on how you interact with colleagues.

Sharing learning through the business

In the meantime, the business has a fabulously engaged group of users who are excelling at gaining value from the technology and in helping others to master the potential benefits. BT Group now hopes to share the fantastic learning through the business. 

Liam Canavan explains, “Copilot has levelled the playing field for our Able2 colleagues. In some cases, people feel they have exceeded the level of their colleagues. They are leading the conversations. Having become Copilot power users, they have begun to teach others how to use and benefit from Copilot.”

For example, Copilot can be used equally successfully for content creation and editing, says Ian Chown. He explains, “Generating a first draft of a document as a standalone document works really well. I like to link it to another document for tone or content. The document will be about 80 percent right.”

“I use Copilot to continue to work on the document and get it the other 20 percent of the way. It works better to edit the tone one paragraph at a time, rather than trying to edit the entire document at once. Continually prompting it, paragraph by paragraph works best for me. It's a rapid, iterative process.”

Tips for successful Copilot use

“For a few weeks, try to have a ‘Copilot first’ mentality on every task,” Ian Chown recommends. “Think: can it do something for me here? This way, you can build your confidence in its ability.”

This does require a different mindset, he warns. For example, for the first month or so Ian Chown added a short disclaimer to his emails to advise they have been drafted using Copilot. This way, colleagues weren’t left wondering when there was a change to the usual tone or style of his replies.

“It's being comfortable with somebody else taking control of the delivery of an answer,” he explains. “Think of prompting as you would think of delegating: I need this e-mail to have this structure, this tone, this content. If you think like this, you gain a better response.”

Rewarding for wider team 

“This project has been very special,” says Liam Canavan. “As IT professionals, we spend a lot of time supporting the platforms our colleagues use. Rarely do we have an opportunity to support our colleagues so directly. It’s quite rare to put that at the forefront of what we are doing and that makes this rollout especially rewarding.”

Howard Watson, Chief Security and Networks Officer and executive sponsor for the Able2 Network, agrees, “Over recent years, I've felt a great sense of pride in BT Group's efforts to modify our workspaces to promote equal chances for individuals with disabilities. Thanks to our collaboration with Microsoft, we've been able to implement Copilot as a viable aid for our colleagues who need it, aiding in task management, streamlining communication, and boosting overall productivity. Together with BT Group's array of tools and support options, Copilot stands as a robust supporter, poised to assist in navigating various workplace obstacles.”

Powering a much-needed conversation

One of the most rewarding aspects of the trial has been to inspire a greater, deeper conversation about accessibility needs at BT Group.

Liam Canavan reports that “Even people who didn’t really talk openly about their needs before have been very open about how Copilot has changed their day-to-day work. It’s been really powerful. There’s a real buzz around Copilot and it’s helping us to understand what other accessibility needs we need to look at.”

Early feedback about the use of Microsoft 365 Copilot highlights how its use can support colleagues with different accessibility needs.
BT Group has identified a clear well-being benefit. Colleagues with diverse accessibility needs feel happier, more supported and more comfortable in their work.

Tüpraş, is the largest industrial company by revenue in Türkiye according to Istanbul Chamber of Industry. With more than 60 years of experience, the company aims to further strengthen its leadership as a carbon neutral energy company in 2050. Guided by its Strategic Transformation Plan, Tüpraş is taking bold steps to digitally transform for a sustainable future. "We can’t change the way energy is produced. Therefore, technologies like Microsoft 365 Copilot have become our focus to empower our teams and improve efficiency," explains Yigit Yeldan, Digital Transformation Manager at Tüpraş.

Integrated technology for seamless adoption

Once Microsoft started integrating artificial intelligence (AI) technology into tools like Outlook, Excel, Teams, Word, and PowerPoint, Tüpraş began exploring how these enhancements could help speed up its daily workflow. 

Data governance played a significant role in the decision-making process. “There are lots of AI engines, but with Microsoft, we have the security of knowing that our data is safe and is handled in ways that comply with government regulations, as well as our internal policies and procedures,” Yeldan explains. “Having already used Microsoft solutions, we were confident in the platform’s data compliance.”

Tüpraş also wanted something that could be implemented quickly and smoothly. Microsoft 365 Copilot works with the tools that employees already use daily, enabling a smoother deployment and adoption process. “Implementing AI technologies may take up to six months to integrate with our tools. With Copilot’s easy integration, it only took one week to get everyone set up,” Yeldan adds. 

To ensure a smooth transition to using AI, Tüpraş approached Copilot adoption with a unique perspective, ensuring that AI tools were made available to all employees from the very beginning, rather than limiting the initial rollout to leadership. The company recognized that widespread usage at the operational level would drive the most significant impact. ‘We believed that empowering employees across all levels with Copilot from day one would maximize efficiency gains and accelerate adoption,’ shares Yeldan. This inclusive approach set Tüpraş apart, as few companies implement AI solutions with full-scale deployment from the outset.

The company also conducted training for over 1,000 employees to familiarize them with Copilot and introduce potential use cases. Transformation teams were established in each department to identify how they could use Copilot, drive adoption, and promote success stories.

Inspiring meaningful change across departments

Soon, departments across the organization started to address their own unique challenges, using Copilot to increase efficiency. “Our finance team uses Microsoft 365 Copilot to generate detailed reports in minutes, a task that used to take significant time to compile in our weekly bulletin,” Yeldan remarks. In addition, the team also uses the AI tool to identify potential compliance issues and assign them automatically to relevant stakeholders for resolution.

Meanwhile, the budget planning team uses Copilot to create forecasts and get suggestions on action plans based on historical data and market trends.

Tüpraş’ human resources (HR) team uses Copilot to summarize interviews, helping recruiters recall key points about candidates’ suitability to specific roles. “We also use it to streamline onboarding for new hires by creating plans tailored to different roles. For example, the needs of a technology professional would be different from a finance employee, and Microsoft 365 Copilot would be able to identify that using our internal data,” shares Büşra Saburlu Sütcü, Head of HR Technologies and Analytics. New hires can also go to Copilot as their resource for frequently asked questions, giving them easy access to company policies, processes, and projects. “Shift to Microsoft 365 Copilot has not only empowered employees but also freed HR teams to focus on strategic initiatives by reducing routine inquiries,” Sütcü adds.

Besides internal improvements, Tüpraş has also seen better relationships with its contractors and customers. Yeldan explains, “Our procurement team uses Copilot to draft and review documents, generate legal requirements based on similar previous contracts, and even compose necessary emails to suppliers.” Moreover, the sales and marketing team can craft quicker and more precise answers to customer queries using AI. “Previously, when they received many requests from commercial customers, they had to follow lengthy procedures: talking to managers, who then talked to other managers. With Copilot, sales teams get an accurate response in minutes,” says Yeldan.

Results that impact the bottom line

With the adoption of Copilot, Tüpraş’ has seen measurable efficiencies across its operations, starting with significant time savings. “Employees who used to spend hours on manual tasks can now complete them in minutes with Microsoft 365 Copilot. This provides efficiency gains, which we estimate translates to 5,000 hours saved monthly across our workforce,” explains Yeldan.

Copilot also saves the company on IT expenses through better resource utilization.  Collaboration improved with meeting summaries and action items automatically generated by Copilot, helping teams keep track of work discussed during meetings. 

The company also sees higher quality strategic planning by leveraging the use of AI. “Because AI can search the web and help us analyze what other companies are doing, we use it to generate ideas and insights to inspire our strategies,” Yeldan notes. “It also speeds up complex tasks like scenario modeling and communications, aside from generating presentations, to pitch these new ideas to the executive team.”

Expanding AI’s role in transformation

Looking ahead, Tüpraş plans to deepen its integration of AI, focusing on predictive analytics and real-time decision-making. “Copilot currently analyzes data and provides insights, but we believe it can do more,” Yeldan explains. “We plan to extend Copilot and integrate it with our existing systems, including Microsoft solutions, in-house applications, and other relevant software. Story Content:
SC Ventures, Standard Chartered’s innovation, fintech investment and ventures arm, is exploring solutions to address the challenges of upskilling an evolving workforce that is being shaped by remote work and shifting demographics. 

In collaboration with INSEAD, SC Ventures used Azure OpenAI Service to build Project Eduverse, a secure, AI-driven platform that delivers a tailored simulations and learning experiences. Project Eduverse has already been used in over 50 use-cases across industries and functions to enhance workforce readiness and enable leaders to manage critical conversations more effectively.

SC Ventures is dedicated to driving innovation within Standard Chartered by building, investing, and validating disruptive business models. It operates as a corporate venture builder, setting up startups to commercialise new ideas.

SC Ventures has leveraged generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) with a focus on using large language models (LLM) to solve complex business problems and work with unstructured data. “Over the years, we’ve experimented with different technical approaches, which has helped us grow comfortable with generative AI,” explains Thorsten Neumann, Venture Technology Lead at SC Ventures. ”We’ve adopted the technology to drive business outcomes, from revenue generation to productivity uplift to risk reduction.” 

This early exposure to GenAI informed one of SC Ventures’ most recent innovation ideas. Earlier this year, the company partnered with INSEAD to create Project Eduverse, an innovative learning platform under incubation. “Technology has transformed education, but human behaviour is hard to change. We still learn best through experience,” reflects Neumann. The team drew on how younger generations are more comfortable with technology but still lack experience in navigating critical conversations. This challenge is compounded by the pressures of remote work and shifting workforce demographics. “We created Project Eduverse for organizations to offer targeted real-life conversational learning content accessible to everyone who wants to roleplay life-like situations,” explains Neumann.

A strategic approach to building an innovative platform

SC Ventures wanted to ensure Project Eduverse was built on a foundation that could scale effectively and securely. “We specifically chose Azure for our AI needs because it met our availability, scalability, security, and data processing needs,” shares Neumann. 

SC Ventures also prioritised security by utilising the Critical Security Controls framework, GitHub for secure development practices, and the Microsoft 365 suite for endpoint and identity protection. “Although the content on Project Eduverse isn’t sensitive or transactional like customer data, there is still a strong emphasis on trust and security. Learners need to know that they can learn in a safe space,” Neumann emphasises. 

By using cloud-based architecture, SC Ventures ensured that Project Eduverse could be seamlessly integrated into existing systems like Microsoft Teams and Viva learning. This integration brings an intuitive learning experience right down to the desktop while maintaining the highest standards of data protection.

Expanding possibilities with AI-driven learning

With Project Eduverse, SC Ventures offers the opportunity to leverage AI-driven learning in upskilling frontline staff, roleplay with people leaders, and preparing their future workforce. “Project Eduverse isn't just about delivering learning content. It’s about creating specific experiences that address real-world challenges,” points out Peter Zemsky, Eli Lilly Chaired Professor of Strategy and Innovation at INSEAD. “The platform enables users to translate knowledge into actionable behaviour through simulations powered by GenAI.” 

For instance, sales leaders looking to drive new account acquisitions can benefit from targeted training that prepares their teams for high-stakes conversations. Simulated conversations with AI trainers enable learners to practice and refine skills in realistic environments, with learners receiving nuanced feedback as they go along.

Project Eduverse’s ability to draw on public data and documents allows it to contextualise training conversations effectively. Neumann explains, “For example, if I'm pitching Project Eduverse to a client, I can prepare with Project Eduverse by using the client’s public financial report to understand their priorities.” This approach ensures that learners are not only well-prepared for meetings but also equipped to handle objections and pivot when necessary.

In being informed by machine learning, AI, and data, the platform tailors experiences to specific organisational needs and ensure relevance of content. It can help organisations implement frameworks like SPIN for sales (a conversation model for high-value selling) or Crucial Conversations for managers (a structured approach for touch conversations), ensuring that learners not only know about these methodologies but can effectively apply them to real-world discourses. 

Project Eduverse is designed to address internal challenges, such as preparing line managers for nuanced conversations like policy changes and performance reviews. Through simulations, Project Eduverse equips leaders with skills to manage their teams more effectively. “Those who manage teams and focus on training and upskilling value the relevancy and scalability of Project Eduverse,” remarks Neumann. “All businesses run in-person training with their frontline staff and leaders, but the continuity is constrained by time, geography, and budgets.” By leveraging AI, SC Ventures ensures that Project Eduverse establishes deep relevance across industries and business functions. 

A transformative journey in upskilling

SC Ventures’ journey in co-creating Project Eduverse has been one of discovery and adaptation. “Classic voice generation models often produce dull, monotonous conversations. We spent considerable time optimising voice generation to achieve a certain flair, natural sounding voice profile, and take on a specific persona,” Neumann highlights. “With attention to such detail, we immerse the learner fully into the education experience.”

As the platform evolves, the team’s focus will remain on enhancing Project Eduverse’s capabilities and expanding the platform’s impact across industries. “We’re building a community of coaches to be part of Project Eduverse platform because they often guide learners and help them reflect on their behaviour. We look to ensure there is a synergy between human coaches and the platform’s AI capabilities,” shares Neumann.

Reflecting on this journey, Zemsky sums up, “Learning used to be about static content delivery, but with AI, it’s about creating dynamic, real-life experiences that truly prepare people for the challenges they face.” SC Ventures looks forward to continuing this transformation, using AI to make learning more interactive, relevant, and effective for the modern workforce.

Lifelong learning is a given in today’s fast-moving environment, where executives must continually grow and adapt to thrive in their careers and play their part in finding solutions to global challenges.

Business education has likewise been evolving at pace, and the International Institute for Management Development (IMD) is at the forefront of this change. The institute has innovated continually since its origins in 1946. It delivers genuinely transformative executive education and degree programs, honing the skills leaders need to manage complexity and developing the mindsets required to lead responsible, dynamic organizations towards a prosperous, sustainable and inclusive world.

IMD’s programs are consistently ranked among the world’s best. With campuses in Lausanne, Switzerland and Singapore, a management development hub in Shenzhen, China and an innovation hub in Cape Town, South Africa, IMD has gained wide recognition for its pioneering approach, closeness to the real world of business and profound, tangible impact.

Blending human intelligence and AI for immersive learning

IMD has always been quick to seize new opportunities afforded by technology. This now includes the development of Generative AI (GenAI) tools and games that complement faculty experts’ deep understanding of human dynamics, bringing human and artificial intelligence together for powerful, immersive learning experiences.

“Generative AI represents a pivotal moment in business education, enabling the creation of truly personalized learning journeys at a scale previously unimaginable. At IMD, we're leveraging this technology to build upon our legacy of innovation and practical learning, ensuring tomorrow's leaders develop the adaptive capabilities needed in an AI-powered world,” says Sarah Toms, Chief Innovation Officer at IMD.

Beyond the timeframe of a program, participants can now continue to engage with IMD’s expertise using GenAI, finding insights relevant to their specific contexts. “Through our suite of GenAI tools, we're extending IMD's thought leadership beyond the traditional program footprint,” Toms explains. “We’re putting world-class insights from IMD directly into our participants' pockets, while providing precise, actionable intelligence about where leaders and organizations need to focus to drive growth and impact.”

IMD is a long-standing Microsoft 365 suite customer, so it was an obvious choice for them to use Microsoft Azure OpenAI Services together with other Microsoft solutions, such as Microsoft 365 Copilot and Copilot Studio, in developing its GenAI capabilities.

“Having Microsoft by our side enables us to bring our innovative ideas to life,” says Carlos Ballester Lafuente, Head of IT Innovation at IMD, “Their powerful toolset shows us the way forward.”

Working with Microsoft to secure proof of value

As a cloud-based business school, IMD is particularly impressed by the quality of the Microsoft architecture, the security and simplicity it offers, and the way Microsoft keeps on creatively improving the tools it provides.

“We are keen to try out new things, yes, but always with one eye on proof of value, meaning the value that is added for participants,” notes Vincent Ballini, Chief Information Officer at IMD. “That is why we trust Microsoft, because its vast offerings allow us to be creative but also let us rely on stable and lasting solutions.”

IMD has already supplied all its faculty and staff with Microsoft 365 Copilot, leading to significant productivity gains in administration, creativity, education and IT. The AI solutions also extend to the pedagogy, “Our goal is to enable faculty and participants to get hands on experience with the latest technology tools so they can immediately see the real-world potential and applications in their organization,” Ballester says.

Microsoft’s Azure-based large language models (LLMs) are enabling IMD to amplify learning outcomes beyond previous constraints of time and place. In Microsoft Copilot Studio, for example, it is possible to compile study content for specific target groups and distribute it to participants quickly and relatively easily. One tailor-made solution that included a dedicated Copilot was ready for colleagues in Singapore to use in just four hours.

Focus on participants

IMD’s learning experiences are scalable, where personalized learning journeys are designed to catalyze transformation and personal growth. One of its GenAI tools is a dedicated learning chatbot participants can use to access teaching resources and insights. IMD’s values – sustainability and diversity, equity and inclusion– are also clearly evident in its GenAI applications. This includes a free game developed and introduced as a companion to its Coursera course — it’s an interactive game that teaches environmental, social and governance (ESG) principles – hosted on Azure.

IMD also provides a hands-on, lab approach to learning in the form of “GenAI sandboxes”. Here, participants experience the latest in GenAI firsthand and develop new, practical AI use cases for their own professional contexts. The AI itself gives the participants direct feedback on their work. “This is a fascinating experiment, because it explores ethical issues and the use of Generative AI,” Ballester explains.

Sarah Toms adds: “We were inspired by the possibilities opened by GenAI right from the start. It is incredible what we have already achieved in collaboration with Microsoft. To maximize the benefits to the organizations and participants who come to IMD, it is vital that we implement these approaches – including our own AI principles – carefully and securely.” IMD has taken care to create a set of principles that serve as a framework for the responsible use of AI, including its ethical, societal and commercial aspects. Leveraging services like Azure AI Content Safety is key to ensure the technical implementation of these principles.

Advancing the transformation together

As a leader in executive education, IMD seeks to constantly iterate and improve its offerings in real time. Its leadership is excited to be collaborating with Microsoft on an ongoing basis, leveraging the latest in GenAI developments, rapidly bringing new capabilities into its pedagogical solutions. IMD uses GenAI to evaluate program results and optimize its work. Questions asked by participants during the courses serve as datasets for future programs, allowing IMD’s faculty to adapt learning to evolving needs.

“We gradually become more intelligent with regard to our teaching content,” explains Louis Leclézio, Chief Operations Officer. “With the aid of GenAI, we can anticipate what participants’ questions.” GenAI records, evaluates and anonymizes every relevant aspect of each course. These findings can then be fed back into the organizations: Where do we currently have the right focus? And where don’t we? What are the key findings, and what are the next steps to take?

A similar approach is adopted in a project to promote key interdisciplinary competencies in IMD’s MBA program. Supported by GenAI, IMD analyzes how well participants perform in transversal skills such as problem solving, pattern recognition and convincing communication. It then produces personalized reports that immediately proposes ways to develop and improve weaker skillsets.

“Having a leading-edge partner like Microsoft helps us to unlock a completely new dimension of intelligence within our programs,” Toms concludes. “Together, we use data to advance the transformation of both individuals and organizations. And we ourselves continue to improve in the process.”

Ground-breaking GenAI strategies for the future of learning

Thanks to its innovative approach and the determination to always optimize itself, IMD is playing a crucial role in shaping the future of learning. This visionary orientation has already been highly influential, with many companies adopting IMD’s AI strategy and principles as the basis for their own initiatives. An open and holistic but also carefully considered AI strategy that gives top priority to the individual learning experience will remain fundamental to IMD’s success.

“Going forward, the analytics and feedback loops that GenAI provides will make our learning journeys even more relevant to individuals,” Toms says. “Using GenAI in conjunction with what we have always excelled at – human-to-human learning that builds communities with responsible foundations – allows us to provide highly impactful technology-mediated learning that breaks through anything that was previously possible.”

Louis Leclézio is in full agreement: “At any age, the more we learn, the more relevant we stay in today’s world. That is why it is so important to us to use Generative AI in an ever-changing world. Thanks to our partnership with Microsoft, our AI solutions can help managerial staff prepare today for the challenges of tomorrow.”

With rapidly changing shopping trends and busy, cost-conscious customers, grocery stores around the world are looking for new ways to make operations efficient and the food shopping experience convenient and cost-effective. Iceland Foods, a fast-growing United Kingdom grocery chain with more than 960 stores and a highly-trafficked online site, is no exception. “The UK food retail sector is fast-paced and dynamic,” says Stuart Bickley, Head of Development at Iceland Foods. “To stay competitive, we must be agile and react quickly to market conditions and consumer trends."

For Iceland Foods, transactional data holds the most value in shaping business decisions, both in-store and online. “It helps us track sales, measure product and promotion performance, identify high traffic times across all stores, and assess inventory and staffing needs,” says Phil Oldfield, Head of Data Engineering at Iceland Foods.

"We wanted to adapt faster by getting that intelligence in real time,” adds Ben Howell, Data Engineer at Iceland Foods.

Data unification and real-time intelligence

Iceland Foods had been using Microsoft Azure, including Azure Synapse Analytics for its data analysis. “We’d been using Azure Synapse Analytics to pull data from different sources for analysis, but it required a lot of data preparation and aggregation, making it difficult to keep pace with demand for insights,” recalls Bickley. As a result, the team spent more time getting data into the system than gaining actionable intelligence. 

Wanting a more automated, unified solution to manage and analyze streaming transactional data, Iceland chose Microsoft Fabric and Fabric Real-Time Intelligence. “We were impressed by Microsoft Fabric and its real-time intelligence innovation,” says Howell. The team also appreciated the unification of Azure services like Power BI, Azure Synapse Analytics, and Azure Data Factory into a single platform. Additionally, Fabric interoperates with Azure AI Foundry, including Azure OpenAI Service, giving the company the ability to use AI-driven analytics for regulatory reporting, risk assessments, and customer insights.

But it was Microsoft Fabric, with its low latency, speed of data intake, and ability to consume large datasets within minutes, that really struck the Iceland Foods IT team. “Fabric delivers a shortcut to the data ingestion process, reducing the need for extensive involvement from other teams,” explains Bickley. “Fabric pulls everything into one place: big data capabilities, SQL database capabilities, real-time intelligence. It massively reduces data movement and preparation, and data is easily shared across different platforms."

Data at the speed of business

Microsoft Fabric and Real-Time Intelligence are also supporting Iceland Foods in other ways, including:

Increased operational efficiency: The unified compute model and data processing capabilities of Fabric have helped Iceland Foods centralize data processes and potentially reduce infrastructure costs.

Enhanced security: With built-in security features, Fabric helps Iceland Foods further safeguard data.

Better collaboration and accessibility: The ability of Fabric to support seamless data flow across Iceland Foods means more people can access, use, and share data more effectively.

Though the project is still in early days, Iceland Foods is already seeing how fast access to data supports fast decision-making. ​For example, Iceland Foods teams can get near real-time details on individual product purchases to aggregated sales data. “This means we can make rapid changes on things like special promotions, inventory, and staffing based on customer needs and shopping trends,” says Oldfield. “We’re getting insights into real-time business performance that just wasn’t possible before.”

With this, Iceland Foods is looking to use Microsoft Fabric at the corporate level as a company-wide reporting and data management solution. Multiple data migrations from on-premises to Fabric are currently underway. “It’s exciting times,” says Bickley. “With Fabric and Real-Time Intelligence, we can keep pace with operational needs and customer trends. We’re getting data at the speed of business.”

Story Content:
Temasek Polytechnic was established in 1990 and is a leading institution of higher learning in Singapore. It offers 36 full-time diploma courses and over 40 part-time programs across its six academic schools, serving 13,000 full-time students. Capitalizing on opportunities and harnessing new technology has helped the polytechnic establish a reputation for its academic programs, hands-on research, strong leadership, and company culture.

"At Temasek Polytechnic, we aim to equip all our students and staff with the latest digital skills, such as those related to artificial intelligence (AI), data analytics, and automation,” shares Peter Lam, Principal & CEO at Temasek Polytechnic. “This will empower them with critical life skills to create, innovate, and make a meaningful impact in their workplace and society.” 

Paving the way for success in a digital world

To nurture citizen developers, Temasek Polytechnic sought to empower staff and students to build applications and solve real-world problems without relying on IT experts. “Normally, we’d need to brief software developers and go through a back-and-forth process because they might not be completely familiar with the business domain,” explains Dr. Eng Pin Kwang, Senior Director, Chief Data Officer, and Chief Information Officer at Temasek Polytechnic. “That’s why having citizen developers with a combination of industry knowledge and access to low-code, no-code tools can lead to faster development and more tailored applications.” 

By empowering citizen developers, the polytechnic hoped to capitalize on opportunities to streamline repetitive tasks, such as scheduling, generating reports, and gathering information. For example, signing up a student for overseas trips, which is a part of their curriculum, would require less effort with automation. Students had to submit several documents, and staff would manually verify details and email each student. “Imagine only having three or four administrators dealing with hundreds or thousands of student registrations—it can be quite challenging,” shares Dr. Eng. 

Another area Temasek Polytechnic aimed to enhance was communication with parents. To keep parents informed about upcoming student events or performances, staff would need to manually send timely notifications. “We saw an opportunity to automate this process, allowing notifications to be triggered automatically thus reducing the risk of errors or delays,” Dr. Eng explains. The polytechnic was looking for a solution that would empower staff to independently innovate and implement changes, ultimately driving overall efficiency.

Since the polytechnic relied on Power BI and Microsoft 365, choosing a solution in the Microsoft environment made the most sense. “We wanted a frictionless transition and a solution that users could learn and pick up very quickly,” says Serena Tai, Director, IT Services at Temasek Polytechnic. This led the institution to adopt the Microsoft Power Platform.  

A transformative adoption journey 

The polytechnic wanted to inspire widespread adoption of the Power Platform among its entire staff, including the teaching staff to integrate these tools into their lessons. “We wanted to equip everyone with the skills needed to create applications that require little to no coding skills as part of their digital competency,” shares Dr. Eng. 

Temasek Polytechnic faculty and administrators were introduced to the Power Platform through structured training sessions, workshops, and hands-on engagements. “We started by communicating our plans to the staff during sessions about upcoming trends, including low-code and no-code technologies,” recalls Serena. These sessions provided opportunities for employees to explore how low-code, no-code tools could be incorporated into their daily work. The polytechnic also organized further in-depth training sessions and events like The Art of Possible ideation workshop, which were venues where employees could identify potential use cases and develop solutions tailored to their needs.

To further solidify the practicality of Power Platform, Temasek Polytechnic organized hackathons for colleagues to work on real use cases. Here, participants could experiment with automating real-world processes and build functional apps.

Besides driving innovation, Temasek Polytechnic also had to ensure security was in place. It established a governance framework to support citizen developer-driven innovation. This includes using Data Loss Prevention (DLP) policies to block high-risk actions and auto-claim policies to auto-assign licenses, as well as setting up controls in the production and sandbox environments. “It’s easy to start something, but sustaining it requires deliberate planning. Using Microsoft’s Center of Excellence solution offers better oversight over the entire Power Platform environment,” explains Serena.

From hackathon to real impact

Fostering employee innovation led to impactful solutions. At the hackathon, Nurzahiah Jumat, Lecturer at the Center for Life Skills, School of Humanities & Social Sciences at Temasek Polytechnic, built the winning app despite having no technical background. Instead of sending mass email announcements manually to students, the app sends personalized assignment reminders. “We’ve saved about 850 hours over the semester,” she says. “In one instance, I sent out 1,600 messages in just three days. Doing this without automation would have taken us about 11 days.”

Students responded even better than anticipated. “Sending one personalized reminder to nudge students to complete their e-learning activities increased the completion rate by 64%,” highlights Jumat. Since then, the automation has been expanded to a larger cohort across multiple subjects.

Another solution handles student requests for editing and proofreading support. All requests now go through an automated system on Power Platform, removing the need for senior managers to manually review each request. 

Tan Cheng Khoon, a Senior Manager at the School of Engineering, had already built a QR code solution to replace manual attendance tracking when he attended the hackathon. “It was clear that if I had built the attendance app on Power Apps from the start, I could’ve developed it much faster and made it compatible across different devices quite easily,” he shares. 

As staff grew more comfortable with the Power Platform, new use cases emerged across departments. “Today, we have over 798,000 workflow runs on the Power Platform and have saved approximately 20,000 man-hours since launching a year ago,” highlights Dr. Eng.

Empowering the next digital generation 

With the success of faculty and staff embracing the Power Platform, Temasek Polytechnic has since shifted gears to introduce codeless development capabilities to students. This includes introducing Microsoft Power Apps into the core curriculum. In the last month, over 5,000 students have used or created applications using Power Apps. 

To give students more practical experience, Temasek Polytechnic has begun exploring new opportunities with Microsoft Copilot Studio. “We had close to 100 students participating in a pilot of Microsoft Copilot Studio through their curriculum. They found the platform easier to use than many similar AI assistants and troubleshooting much simpler,” shares Serena.

The polytechnic is also the first in Singapore to introduce a specialist diploma in low-code app development for business into its academic portfolio as a continuous education programming option for adult learners. “By bringing in new technologies into the curriculum, we ensure that our students are trained in what the industry needs. It helps us achieve our mission of giving students the technical know-how and practical skills to boost their employability and set them up for success right out of the gate,” Dr. Eng explains. 

As digital tools evolve, Temasek Polytechnic remains committed to lifelong learning. In 2025, the polytechnic hopes to initiate a Community of Practice to provide structured support and foster best practices in low-code, no-code, and AI. It will also explore new tools and features such as the AI builder in the Power Platform in anticipation of even more developer-driven innovation. “Ensuring the availability of technology is important for our future. By making these resources readily available, we can educate and empower our staff and students to use them effectively,” concludes Serena.

Navigating an ocean of legal information

To best support their sector-leading global wealth management enterprise, UBS’s in-house lawyers and legal experts needed to effectively search legal documents across multiple languages.

“Our internal document library contains about 26 million documents,” explains Vlad Stoian, Product Owner for the Legal AI Assistant at UBS. “Finding specific knowledge in this vast repository was like finding a particular grain of sand on the beach.”

The search tools in place weren’t up to the task. “It took lots of manual work to do things like searching provisions across funds,” says Felicia Efta, Legal Counsel Asset Management, Head of Alternative Funds EMEA at UBS.

Improving legal workflows with Azure AI knowledge retrieval

UBS sought to empower its legal team to focus on more value-added work and streamline the time spent searching through documents. The company chose to build its solution on Microsoft Azure OpenAI Service and Azure AI Search. The resulting knowledge management solution, Legal AI Assistant (LAIA), offers semantic search functionality at scale using metadata identification from the underlying storage systems.

“The AI assistant vectorizes language in existing documents, grouping related concepts together,” explains Stoian. “It can understand natural language and pick up on synonyms and semantic similarities. For instance, if someone searches ‘remaining part,’ LAIA can find ‘legacy portfolio.’ It lets employees enter descriptive text, rather than just keywords.”

LAIA points employees to relevant paragraphs from millions of documents, highlighting key information while maintaining appropriate document-level security protections. “LAIA respects access rights by ensuring people only search and access documents they’re authorized to view,” says Stoian. “Microsoft technology has helped us respect document-level access in a consistent way, which was essential given our large volume of files.”

UBS is expanding the tool globally, all while respecting the tight regulations placed on the industry, along with the needs of its employees. “Moving to a system like this takes training,” says Efta. “We need to switch from keyword search to descriptive search and learn prompting skills. That’s why we’ve also developed bespoke training focused on helping employees to improve their queries and better utilize LAIA.”

Microsoft supported UBS with technical guidance to ensure success throughout the development and deployment process. “We did a lot of upfront planning to ensure the solution would fit within the highly regulated UBS environment and work for our use case,” says Ilias Fotopoulos, Chapter Lead, AI & Data Engineer at UBS.

Fotopoulos was impressed by how Microsoft technology facilitated the solution UBS needed. “At UBS, we were early adopters of Azure AI technologies, and they’ve only gotten better over time,” he says. “They’ve helped us streamline search across millions of documents at scale and with speed.”

Transforming information access and delivering AI-powered search

With the implementation of the Legal AI Assistant, UBS has transformed its knowledge retrieval processes, and lawyers can easily access stored information in a fraction of the time it used to take. UBS legal experts can now conduct complex queries within minutes, not hours, across the vast document repository. This efficiency is freeing up employees to focus on higher-value tasks. 

“Deploying Microsoft AI technologies has made our legal teams’ work easier and faster,” says Stoian. “We plan to enhance LAIA further by converting unstructured data to structured data to make it easier to search and filter documents based on specific criteria. We want to keep unlocking more use cases and improve LAIA’s overall utility.”


“The performance of Azure AI Search exceeded our initial prototype’s results, and it’s helped us build one of the largest-scale knowledge retrieval systems at UBS,” says Fotopoulos. “That just reinforces our certainty that collaborating with Microsoft on this project was the right decision.”

Addressing complexity in modern manufacturing

At Sandvik, innovation is at the core of operations. The company develops cutting-edge technology solutions that power modern manufacturing. However, there is a growing skills gap in the industry, increased component complexity, rising automation, and a younger workforce with new expectations.

To address this, Sandvik is using Microsoft Cloud for Manufacturing across its manufacturing software brands. It develops its products with GitHub Copilot, and has used Azure OpenAI Service and Azure AI Search to create its proprietary Manufacturing Copilot, a tool used by its customers and its sales and customer support teams.

Sandvik has never shied away from innovation. But AI’s ability to turn human expertise into instantly accessible intelligence marked a significant shift.

“We needed to utilize smart technology globally while still supporting our customers,” explains Magnus Malmström, Chief Technology Officer of Sandvik Manufacturing Solutions. “That’s why we used Microsoft Cloud for Manufacturing to develop the Manufacturing Copilot.”

Scaling AI at Sandvik

Rolling out the Manufacturing Copilot across Sandvik’s CAM software brands required a strategic approach. Instead of building a separate solution for its different products, Sandvik created a shared service on which the company built product-specific Manufacturing Copilots.

Each solution was trained on proprietary knowledge, unique to each brand, so users have access to product documentation, help files, and audio/video recordings. They are further trained on technical support continuously and eventually connect with each other to bring even more intelligence to the shop floor.

With the Manufacturing Copilot, Sandvik employees and its customers can quickly access decades of company knowledge using natural language. The tool was first launched in Sandvik’s CAD/CAM software Cimatron, GibbsCAM, and SigmaNEST and will soon be accessible for 400,000 users.

The results? “Manufacturing Copilot saves time for our employees, on average, close to 20% to 30%, and if it is something completely new that we are facing for the first time, probably up to 50%,” says Coşkun İslam, Head of Collective Intelligence Engineering at Sandvik Manufacturing Solutions.

Beyond streamlining access to information, AI is helping reduce language barriers. “We support 19 languages with special algorithms for domain-specific language translation, ensuring users can interact in their own language,” İslam explains. This helps with global collaboration and access to information in the user’s own language.

AI in sales and support

Internally, Sandvik employees also use the tool in areas like sales, customer support, and training. “Onboarding a new salesperson now takes about half the time using the Manufacturing Copilot,” says Joe Ulrich, Regional Sales Manager at SigmaNEST, one of Sandvik’s brands.

Providing immediate, accurate answers during sales calls has enhanced customer confidence and decision-making. The tool helps Ulrich to eliminate follow-up meetings, keeping the sales process moving. “If I can answer a customer’s question during a sales meeting with the Manufacturing Copilot, it saves so much time and increases my chance of winning a deal,” Ulrich says.

Robert Choudury, Application Engineer at SigmaNEST, also uses the tool to provide customer support. With the Manufacturing Copilot, “We also learn from the direct customer feedback loop so we can resolve issues faster and have access to support in real time,” he says.

The future of AI at Sandvik

As AI evolves, so does Sandvik’s vision. Beyond efficiency, AI is transforming how expertise is shared and preserved. “This technology unites people with physical human knowledge and tech competence,” Malmström says.

As industries transform through automation and AI, Sandvik remains at the forefront. The Manufacturing Copilot isn’t just a tool—it’s a catalyst for change. By turning complex expertise into instantly accessible knowledge, it helps Sandvik engineers, developers, customer-facing teams, and customers work smarter and faster than ever.

With Microsoft Cloud for Manufacturing, Sandvik is proving that the future of manufacturing isn’t just automated—it’s intelligent, adaptive, and deeply human.

The Craneware Group transforms healthcare with data-driven insights

The Craneware Group, a global healthcare technology company, is dedicated to improving financial and operational performance for healthcare providers. Founded in 1999, the company has grown to serve over 12,000 hospitals, clinics, and affiliated retail pharmacies, impacting nearly 200 million unique patient encounters every year.

The Craneware Group has an unwavering commitment to their mission of improving financial and operational performance so healthcare providers can focus on delivering better care for patients. Founded to help automate the process of turning care into claims through chargemaster technology, they’ve expanded to provide a cloud-based advanced analytics, automation, and compliance platform called Trisus®. This dedication to innovation and their impact on the success of healthcare providers make The Craneware Group a trusted industry partner.

"It's about improving performance in all areas of the business of healthcare so hospitals can take better care of their patients. Everyone deserves the best healthcare possible, and we're part of that at The Craneware Group," said Maggie Tubassum, Vice President Trisus Platform at The Craneware Group.

Tackling data disparity

A strategic acquisition by The Craneware Group introduced new applications and data sets to further enhance the company’s financial and operational solution offerings. Like many of their customers, The Craneware Group faced the challenge of unifying disparate data from new sources into their Trisus platforms, as the newly acquired assets were developed on Oracle.

The function of the Trisus platform is to centralize value cycle data from care settings—including hospital and post-discharge activities—to create a unified view of the patient journey. This level of data integration is a core strength and hallmark of the company’s expertise, enabling healthcare providers to bolster revenue integrity, perform cost and margin analyses, and meet compliance requirements, all while improving patient outcomes and reducing healthcare costs. With one of the largest databases of US healthcare data outside the insurance market, the company needed a solution to seamlessly incorporate the newly acquired data on Oracle into Trisus.

Unifying healthcare data

To address this challenge, The Craneware Group leveraged Oracle Database@Azure to centralize their data, particularly after acquiring a company with a significant Oracle-based 340B data system. Migrating allowed them to continue leveraging the processing power of Oracle, while also reducing latency and improving data integration across other products and services they were using. Additionally, they utilized Azure SQL Database and Azure Cosmos DB to store and manage various types of healthcare data, providing a robust and scalable solution. Centralizing their data allows them to get a holistic look at their customer’s most pressing concern: the end-to-end patient journey, from a hospital stay and all that entails, to the outpatient pharmacy to fill prescriptions. This level of detail from The Craneware Group empowers healthcare leaders to optimize care and better serve their communities. To gain even deeper insights, The Craneware Group has started using machine learning for predictive analytics, leveraging the models available through Azure OpenAI Service.

"Oracle Database@Azure has been a strategic asset for us. It allows us to leverage the best of both worlds—Oracle's robust database services and Azure's high-performance cloud infrastructure. This integration makes it easier for us to uncover actionable insights from our data," said Abhilesh Gandhi, Chief Technology Officer at The Craneware Group.

Gaining deeper insights for better healthcare

As deployment continues to ramp up, The Craneware Group has already seen benefits of this project, including reduced licensing costs and improved healthcare data analytics. This is just the beginning. They plan to enhance their Azure infrastructure with managed solutions and AI for deeper healthcare insights. Utilizing Microsoft Fabric as a mesh to integrate Oracle, SQL, and Cosmos DB, they aim to create a comprehensive data view to improve data analysis and enable them to build out customer large language models and open up more pathways to leverage AI. Moving their VMware virtual machines to Azure VMware Solution will free them from managing infrastructure as a service. By gaining deeper insights into the patient’s journey, they aim to be a trusted partner to healthcare organizations across the US, transforming the business of healthcare.

When Marija Grujic was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis after childbirth, her life took an unexpected turn. Marija attended specialized neurorehabilitation clinics that used gamified rehabilitation to stimulate her vision and encourage physical activity. "I was much better after one month course of rehabilitation. I had much more strength, and my walking was noticeably better," recalls Marija Grujic, Chief Executive Officer and Co-Founder of Neuroblast. “But two months later, my condition started to deteriorate again.”

“Treating neurodegenerative diseases can be costly and complex,” adds Marko Grujic, Marija’s husband and Chief Technology Officer and Co-Founder of Neuroblast. “For one, you need to constantly go to rehab clinics. Then there’s also prescription medication which sometimes has unwanted side effects. After all that, you’re not even sure if the therapies will be effective.”

Marko was determined to find a way to help Marija. Observing the clinics' methods, the Grujics noticed that while the mechanics and workouts were effective, the games lacked engagement and there was no feedback mechanism to monitor cognitive changes. Marko, a hardware and software engineer with over 20 years of experience, decided to leverage his expertise to create a home-based solution for Marija. 

This became the start of Neuroblast. Grujics assembled a team that included specialists in electronics and biomechanics. Within a few months, the group developed the first prototypes of their rehabilitative devices. Marija soon began using the prototypes at home alongside personalized training programs on a Neuroblast developed interface, experiencing improvements without the high daily clinic costs. The devices include a standing board to train strength and stability, as well as a 3D camera that tracks finger and hand movement to ensure she performs her exercises correctly.

Finding critical support on multiple fronts

To bring Neuroblast’s solutions to more people, Marko needed robust technological support and decided to work with Microsoft to develop its devices. The company implemented Visual Studio to write code and develop its Unity video games. GitHub Enterprise was also important for storing and managing code, while Microsoft Azure became the main cloud system for Neuroblast, which the company used to host its app. 

"It’s really helpful to have all the services we need in one ecosystem," Marko Grujic notes. The Grujics also found financial and mentoring support through the Microsoft Founders Hub, which enabled the team to grow and scale. Being part of the Founders Hub helped Marko navigate the startup ecosystem. He gained access to expert engineers for technical advice and picked up practical tips from other founders within the program.

"Everyone was saying that I needed to show a business plan, map projections, and more. I knew what we wanted to achieve but struggled with getting all the paperwork done,” recalls Marko. “With help from more experienced founders, as well as Microsoft 365 Copilot, I’m able to draft the presentations and documentation for all the various institutions, programs, and conferences with ease," he shares.

Helping people across the world

With a vision to serve customers all over the world, Neuroblast carefully considered how it could make its application accessible while protecting and storing medical data appropriately. “We chose to host all of our programs on Azure, which ensures that personal information is stored in data centers based on the user’s nationality and complies with the local data residency laws,” explains Marko. 

Neuroblast was founded with a clear focus—to develop a suite of devices that assist persons with neurodegenerative disorders, as well as their healthcare providers, in rehabilitation. Early in its journey, the company developed Motus, a controller that can be worn on the hand, foot, or leg. The device tracks movement in 3D space, translating it into a video game for users to engage in interactive exercises that promote coordination and mobility.

The company then went on to develop two other devices. Visio, a visual hand-tracking device; and Terra, a smart carpet that measures pressure to gauge muscle strength. Alongside these devices, Neuroblast introduced brain wave scanning to measure the effectiveness of rehabilitation exercises. The company uses artificial intelligence (AI) to ingest and analyze data, which is collected every time a person uses one of their devices. Marko says, "We knew that analyzing six months of daily exercise data manually just wouldn’t be sustainable. Azure OpenAI Service enables us to process data efficiently and personalize reports.”

Neuroblast delivers exercise programs through a visual interface on its app. Those who don’t speak English can interact with an AI avatar in their native language, which can be critical when describing important procedures. “When we were testing out the devices in a New York hospital, we’ve had physicians come to us asking if we can tailor the instructions to non-English speakers. With Azure OpenAI, we can do that quickly,” says Marko. The AI avatar explains the workouts, what they’re for, how to do them, and why they’re important. This ensures that people are doing the exercises safely and effectively. It also helps users stick to the exercise program more consistently, helping them experience results sooner and lead to better outcomes.

Motivating patients to stay active

Since its inception, Neuroblast has developed several devices to aid rehabilitation for persons with neurodegenerative disorders, as well as their healthcare providers. These devices are integrated with interactive video games, enabling Neuroblast to enhance patient engagement while potentially providing valuable up-to-date information to healthcare providers. Neuroblast’s holistic approach aims to improve the effectiveness of rehabilitation and reduce the progression of neurodegenerative diseases. For people with neurodegenerative diseases like Marija, the impact of Neuroblast can be life changing.

"I told my doctors about Neuroblast two years ago when I started using the prototype," Marija recalls. Initially, her doctors were skeptical. Soon, these same physicians realized that the devices kept her motivated to be active and contributed to positive outcomes. Marija has seen significant improvements since using Neuroblast devices. "I’m walking now, working out at the gym, and going out of the house every day. Three years ago, this wasn’t possible. Sometimes, I couldn’t even get out of bed," she shares.

This positive result is, in part, because Neuroblast’s rehabilitative exercise programs adapt to each person’s condition by relying on AI to adjust difficulty levels. "We don’t want the game to overwhelm users. If it recognizes that you’re having a bad day—which often happens with neurodegenerative diseases—it will automatically decrease the difficulty of the game," Marko notes. “Alternatively, if you’re doing really well, the game will increase the difficulty, because nobody wants to work out if it doesn’t feel rewarding.” 

Future plans and collaborations

Neuroblast is focused on expanding its impact and refining its technology, while still relying on Microsoft solutions.  Neuroblast plans to conduct a study with customers using its devices, to determine if they contribute to higher activation of the cerebral cortex—the part of the brain that regulates conscious activity—during rehabilitation, which would indicate improved outcomes. 

Neuroblast is also exploring innovative applications for its technology. "Two months ago, we were contacted by an institute in Serbia, asking if Visio—Neuroblast’s hand tracking device—could be used to monitor surgeons’ hands during operations," Marko says. This collaboration could lead to enhanced surgical training through virtual environments, where students could practice complex procedures using Visio camera and tailored surgical scenarios based on Neuroblast’s game architecture.

For Marija, the accessibility of Neuroblast devices and solutions is the main priority. "We gladly work with clinics and pharmaceutical companies, but we don’t have exit plans like many other startups. This is a deeply personal endeavor, and we want to bring the benefits that I enjoy at home to as many people as we can,” she concludes.
